question: Northern Trail Outfitters has a requirement to encrypt a few widely used standard fields. They also want to be able to use these fields in workflow rules. Which security solution should an Integration Architect recommend to fulfill the business use case?
optionA: Cryptography Class
optionB: Data Mask
optionC: Classic Encryption
optionD: Shield Platform Encryption
explanation:
Shield Platform Encryption encrypts data at rest with AES-256 and is the only option that encrypts standard fields while preserving platform functionality — workflow rules, validation rules and approval processes keep working on supported field types.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Cryptography Class) — an Apex toolkit of crypto primitives for hand-rolled encryption, not a field-level feature.
Option B (Data Mask) — anonymises sandbox data; it encrypts nothing in production.
Option C (Classic Encryption) — custom text fields only, so it cannot reach standard fields, and workflow rules can't use it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_pe_standard_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What should an Architect recommend to ensure all integrations to the Northern Trail Outfitters company portal use SSL mutual authentication?
optionA: Enable My Domain and SSL/TLS.
optionB: Enforce SSL/TLS Mutual Authentication.
optionC: Generate a self-signed certificate.
optionD: Generate a CA-signed certificate.
explanation:
Enabling the "Enforce SSL/TLS Mutual Authentication" user permission and assigning it to the integration users forces inbound API connections to authenticate on port 8443 with a client certificate — which is what "mutual" requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Enable My Domain and SSL/TLS) — gives one-way TLS, where only the server proves identity.
Option C (Generate a self-signed certificate) — creates a credential but enforces nothing.
Option D (Generate a CA-signed certificate) — same gap; a prerequisite step, not the control.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_keys_uploading_mutual_auth_cert_api.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is planning to create a native employee-facing mobile app with the look and feel of Salesforce Lightning Experience. The mobile app needs to integrate with NTO's Salesforce org. Which Salesforce API should be used to implement this integration?
optionA: User Interface API
optionB: REST API
optionC: Connect REST API
explanation:
User Interface API is purpose-built for native clients recreating the Lightning Experience look and feel: it returns records, layouts, picklist values, theming and metadata in one response, so the app renders Salesforce screens without reimplementing them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (REST API) — returns raw data only, leaving the app to rebuild layout and metadata logic itself.
Option C (Connect REST API) — scoped to Chatter, feeds and social objects, not general record and layout data.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.uiapi.meta/uiapi/ui_api_get_started.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters needs to present shipping costs and estimated delivery times to their customers. Shipping services used vary by region and have similar but distinct service request parameters. Which integration component capability should be used?
optionA: Enterprise Service Bus to determine which shipping service to use, and transform requests to the necessary format.
optionB: Outbound Messaging to request costs and delivery times from shipper delivery services with automated error retry.
optionC: Apex REST Service to implement routing logic to the various shipping services.
optionD: Enterprise Service Bus user interface to collect shipper-specific form data.
explanation:
An Enterprise Service Bus supplies the routing, mediation and transformation this needs: Salesforce calls one canonical endpoint, and the ESB picks the regional carrier and reshapes the request into that carrier's format.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Outbound Messaging) — fire-and-forget SOAP with a fixed message shape, no transformation, and no reply to show the customer.
Option C (Apex REST Service) — exposes Salesforce as a provider for inbound calls; this requirement is outbound.
Option D (ESB user interface) — an ESB is middleware and presents no end-user data-entry forms.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: What is the first thing an Integration Architect should validate if a callout from a Lightning Web Component to an external endpoint is failing?
optionA: The endpoint domain has been added to Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.
optionB: The endpoint URL has been added to CSP Trusted Sites (Content Security Policies).
optionC: The endpoint URL has been added to an outbound firewall rule.
optionD: The endpoint URL has been added to Remote Site Settings.
explanation:
A Lightning Web Component calling an external endpoint from JavaScript is subject to Salesforce's Content Security Policy first: unless the URL is in CSP Trusted Sites, the browser blocks the request before it leaves the page.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) — the CORS allowlist governs inbound calls into Salesforce, not outbound ones.
Option C (outbound firewall rule) — a network control; this failure happens inside the browser.
Option D (Remote Site Settings) — authorises Apex server-side callouts, which a client-side fetch never consults.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_trusted_urls_manage.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A company that is a leading provider of training delivers courses to students globally. The company decided to use a Customer Community in order to allow students to log in to the community, register for courses, and pay course fees. The company has a payment gateway that takes more than 30 seconds to process the payment transaction. Students would like to get the payment result in real-time so in case an error happens, they can retry the payment process. What is the recommended integration approach to process payments based on this requirement?
optionA: Use a Platform Event to process payment to the payment gateway.
optionB: Use Continuation to process payment to the payment gateway.
optionC: Use Change Data Capture to process payment to the payment gateway.
optionD: Use Request and Reply to make an API call to the payment gateway.
explanation:
Continuation is built for a long-running callout the user must wait on: it suspends the Visualforce, Aura or LWC request, hands the callout to the Continuation server and resumes in a callback, supporting callouts up to 120 seconds — comfortably covering a gateway that takes more than 30.
Note that the usual reason given for rejecting Request-and-Reply is wrong. There is no "10-second ceiling": Salesforce documents 10 seconds as the default Apex callout timeout and setTimeout() raises it to 120. The real problem is that a synchronous callout holds the application server thread for the whole wait, and any request over 5 seconds counts against the org-wide concurrent long-running request limit — which a community of students paying at once would exhaust.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Platform Event) — asynchronous, so it cannot return the payment result to the waiting student.
Option C (Change Data Capture) — publishes record-change notifications; it neither calls a gateway nor replies to a browser.
Option D (Request and Reply) — right interaction shape, but it exhausts the concurrent long-running request limit at this scale (see above).
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_continuation_overview.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_continuation_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands. The explanation asserted a "10-second synchronous Apex callout governor"; Salesforce documents 10 seconds as the default callout timeout, raisable to 120 seconds via setTimeout(). Continuation wins because it releases the application server thread and avoids the concurrent long-running request limit, not because of a ceiling that does not exist. Same correction already applied to the Outbound Messaging question in this deck.

question: An Integration Developer is developing an HR synchronization app for a client. The app synchronizes Salesforce record data changes with an HR system external to Salesforce. What should the integration architect recommend to ensure notifications are stored for up to three days if data replication fails?
optionA: Change Data Capture
optionB: Generic Events
optionC: Platform Events
optionD: Callouts
explanation:
Change Data Capture is purpose-built for keeping an external system in step with Salesforce records: it publishes create, update, delete and undelete events automatically, and Salesforce retains them on the event bus for three days, so a failed subscriber can resume from its stored ReplayId inside that window.
Retention is not what separates it from platform events — both share the same 72-hour retention. Origin is: change events are generated from record changes automatically, whereas platform events must be defined and published explicitly.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Generic Events) — carry an arbitrary payload and no record context.
Option C (Platform Events) — same 72-hour retention, but require you to define the event and publish it by hand.
Option D (Callouts) — point-to-point requests with no durability; a failure stores nothing to replay.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_subscribe_delivery.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/pub-sub-api/guide/event-message-durability.html

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation claimed platform events have "shorter retention (72 hours for high-volume events)", which is self-contradictory — 72 hours is three days — and wrong, since platform events and change events share the same event-bus retention. The real discriminator is that CDC generates change events from record changes automatically.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has recently implemented middleware for orchestration of services across platforms. The ERP system requires transactions be captured near real-time at a REST endpoint initiated in Salesforce when creating an Order. Additionally, the Salesforce team has limited development resources and requires a low-code solution. Which two options will fulfill the use case requirements? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use a Remote Process Invocation – Fire and Forget pattern on insert of the Order using Flow Builder.
optionB: Implement a Workflow Rule with Outbound Messaging to send SOAP messages to the designated endpoint.
optionC: Implement Change Data Capture on the Order object and leverage the ReplayId in the middleware solution.
optionD: Use Process Builder to create a Platform Event, selecting the record type as the Platform Event name on insert of the record.
explanation:
Two low-code paths fit. Flow Builder's HTTP Callout action (A) is a declarative Remote Process Invocation – Fire and Forget to a REST endpoint on Order insert. Change Data Capture (C) publishes Order changes to a streaming channel the middleware subscribes to, using the ReplayId to recover after a disconnect — again with no Apex.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Workflow Rule with Outbound Messaging) — sends SOAP, and the ERP requires REST; low-code and near real-time, so the protocol is the only thing wrong with it.
Option D (Process Builder platform event by record type) — a platform event is a separate sObject you define; a record type cannot be selected as one.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--fire-and-forget
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_subscribe_delivery.htm

question: A large enterprise customer has decided to implement Salesforce as their CRM. The current system landscape includes (1) an ERP solution responsible for customer invoicing and order fulfillment and (2) a Marketing solution used for email campaigns. The customer needs their sales and service associates to use Salesforce to view and log their interactions with customers and prospects. Which system should be the system of record for their customers and prospects?
optionA: ERP with all prospect data from Marketing and Salesforce.
optionB: Marketing with all customer data from Salesforce and ERP.
optionC: Salesforce with relevant Marketing and ERP information.
optionD: A new custom database for customers and prospects.
explanation:
The system of record is the system whose users do the daily lifecycle work on that entity. Sales and service associates work in Salesforce, so Salesforce owns the customer and prospect master, while ERP stays the system of record for invoices and orders and Marketing for campaigns.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ERP) — an invoicing and fulfilment system with no lead, contact or activity model for CRM users.
Option B (Marketing) — owns campaigns, not the customer lifecycle the associates work through.
Option D (a new custom database) — adds a system and a sync problem without solving a business need.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) uses a custom mobile app to interact with their customers. One of the features of the app is Salesforce Chatter feeds. NTO wants to automatically post a Chatter item to Twitter whenever the post includes the #thanksNTO hashtag. Which API should an Integration Architect use to meet this requirement?
optionA: Connect REST API
optionB: REST API
optionC: Streaming API
optionD: Apex REST
explanation:
Connect REST API is the Chatter and Communities API: it exposes feed items, mentions, comments and rich body parsing in a feed-aware way, so a worker can read posts carrying the hashtag and forward them to Twitter.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (REST API) — treats FeedItem as a generic sObject, with none of the feed-rendering helpers.
Option C (Streaming API) — pushes notifications but cannot inspect or post feed content.
Option D (Apex REST) — builds custom inbound endpoints; it is not a way to read Chatter.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.chatterapi.meta/chatterapi/intro_using_chatter_connect.htm

question: An architect recommended using Apex code to make callouts to an external system to process insurance quotes. What should the integration architect consider to make sure this is the right option for the integration?
optionA: The maximum number of callouts in a single Apex transaction.
optionB: The maximum number of parallel Apex callouts in a single Continuation.
optionC: The limit on long-running requests (total execution time).
optionD: The limit of pending operations in the same transaction.
explanation:
Apex enforces a hard governor limit of 100 callouts per transaction, so a quote process that fans out to several endpoints can hit that ceiling — the design has to be sized against it, with batching or queueing if needed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (parallel callouts in a single Continuation) — only relevant if Continuation is the chosen pattern, which it is not here.
Option C (long-running request limit) — concerns cumulative execution time and is rarely the first constraint reached.
Option D (pending operations in the same transaction) — governs queued asynchronous work, not how many callouts a transaction may make.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_gov_limits.htm

question: Which WSDL should an architect consider when creating an integration that might be used for more than one Salesforce organization with different metadata?
optionA: Corporate WSDL
optionB: Partner WSDL
optionC: SOAP API WSDL
optionD: Enterprise WSDL
explanation:
Partner WSDL is loosely typed and generic: records travel as name/value sObject pairs, so one integration works against any org's schema regardless of its metadata.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Corporate WSDL) — not a WSDL Salesforce publishes; the choice is Enterprise or Partner.
Option C (SOAP API WSDL) — a generic label rather than one of the two org-specific WSDLs the question is asking between.
Option D (Enterprise WSDL) — strongly typed and bound to the metadata of the org that generated it, so it breaks as soon as two orgs differ.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_partner.htm

question: Only authorized users are allowed access to the EBS and the Enterprise DMS. Customers call Customer Support when they need clarification on their bills. Customer Support needs seamless access to customer billing information from the EBS and to view generated bills from the DMS. Which three authorization and authentication needs should an integration consultant consider while integrating the DMS and EBS with Salesforce? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Users should be authorized to view information specific to the customer they are servicing without needing to search for that customer.
optionB: Identify options to maintain DMS and EBS authentication and authorization details in Salesforce.
optionC: Consider enterprise security needs for access to DMS and EBS.
optionD: Consider options to migrate DMS and EBS into Salesforce.
optionE: Users should be authenticated into DMS and EBS without having to enter username and password.
explanation:
Context-driven authorisation (A) scopes the call to the customer the agent is already servicing, so no wider search or access is needed. Enterprise security needs (C) capture the encryption, IP allow-listing and audit obligations that apply to billing data. Seamless authentication into both back-ends (E) removes per-system credentials, typically via SAML or OAuth.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (maintain DMS and EBS auth details in Salesforce) — a soft distractor rather than a falsehood. Named Credentials genuinely are how you hold those credentials, and often how E is achieved; it is marked wrong because the question asks what to consider, and B jumps to an implementation choice that sits awkwardly with least privilege when the back-ends already restrict access per user.
Option D (migrate DMS and EBS into Salesforce) — a migration decision, not an authentication or authorisation concern.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5

question: A company needs to integrate a legacy on-premise application that can only support SOAP API. After evaluating the requirements and volume, the Integration Architect determined that the Fire and Forget integration pattern will be most appropriate for sending data from Salesforce to the external application, and getting a response back in a strongly typed format. Which integration capabilities should be used to integrate the two systems?
optionA: Outbound Message for Salesforce → Legacy direction, and SOAP API using Enterprise WSDL for the communication back from the legacy system to Salesforce.
optionB: Platform Events for Salesforce → Legacy direction, and SOAP API using Partner WSDL for the communication back from the legacy system to Salesforce.
optionC: Platform Events for Salesforce → Legacy direction, and SOAP API using Enterprise WSDL for the communication back from the legacy system to Salesforce.
optionD: Outbound Message for Salesforce → Legacy direction, and SOAP API using Partner WSDL for the communication back from the legacy system to Salesforce.
explanation:
Outbound Message is the declarative SOAP Fire-and-Forget mechanism, which matches the SOAP-only legacy constraint without Apex. For the return trip, Enterprise WSDL gives the strongly typed contract the legacy app needs to deserialise sObjects with compile-time type safety.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Platform Events out, Partner WSDL back) — wrong on both halves: events are not SOAP, and Partner WSDL is loosely typed.
Option C (Platform Events out, Enterprise WSDL back) — the return trip is right, but a legacy system that supports only SOAP cannot subscribe to platform events.
Option D (Outbound Message out, Partner WSDL back) — the outbound half is right, but Partner WSDL loses the strongly typed format the requirement names.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_partner.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--fire-and-forget

question: A customer of Salesforce has used Platform Events to integrate their Salesforce instance with an external third-party Artificial Intelligence (AI) system. The AI system provides a prediction score for each lead that is received by Salesforce. Once the prediction score is received, the lead information is saved to Platform Events for other processes. The trigger on the Platform Event is failing once this was rolled out to Production. What type of monitoring should the Integration Consultant have considered to monitor this integration?
optionA: Monitor Platform Events created per hour limits across the Salesforce instance.
optionB: Set up debug logs for Platform Event triggers to monitor performance.
optionC: Validate the Platform Event definition matches the Lead definition.
optionD: Monitor the volume of leads that are created in Salesforce.
explanation:
Platform Events carry hourly publish and delivery allocations that vary by edition and license. When production traffic exceeds them, publishes start failing and downstream triggers stop firing — exactly the symptom described, and the thing to monitor.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (debug logs for the trigger) — a development aid, not a production monitoring strategy, and it does not surface allocation exhaustion.
Option C (validate the event definition matches Lead) — a definition mismatch fails at deploy time, not intermittently after rollout, and no event is required to mirror Lead.
Option D (monitor lead volume) — a proxy at best; the constraint lives at the event bus, not on the Lead object.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_event_limits.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) currently owns a middleware tool and they have developed an API-led integration architecture with three API tiers. The first tier interfaces directly with the systems of engagement, the second tier implements business logic and aggregates data, and the third tier interfaces directly with systems of record. Some of the systems of engagement will be a mobile application, a web application, and Salesforce. UC has a business requirement to return data to the systems of engagement in different formats while also enforcing different security protocols. What should an Integration Architect recommend to meet these requirements?
optionA: Enforce separate security protocols and return formats at the first tier of the API-led architecture.
optionB: Implement an API gateway that all systems of engagement must interface with first.
optionC: Enforce separate security protocols and return formats at the second tier of the API-led architecture.
optionD: Leverage an Identity Provider solution that communicates with the API tiers via SAML.
explanation:
In API-led connectivity the first tier, the Experience layer, exists to tailor responses and security to each consuming channel — mobile, web and Salesforce each get their own shape and auth posture.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an API gateway in front of everything) — a different pattern that does not use the three-tier investment UC has already made.
Option C (enforce it at the second tier) — the Process layer holds business logic; putting channel concerns there couples the two.
Option D (Identity Provider over SAML) — federates user identity, but does nothing about per-channel response formats.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity

question: Northern Trail Outfitters has a registration system that is used for workshops offered at its conferences. Attendees use a Salesforce community to register for workshops, but the scheduling system manages workshop availability based on room capacity. It is expected that there will be a big surge of requests for workshop reservations when the conference schedule goes live. Which integration pattern should be used to manage the influx in registrations?
optionA: Remote Process Invocation – Request and Reply
optionB: Remote Process Invocation – Fire and Forget
optionC: Batch Data Synchronization
optionD: Remote Call-In
explanation:
Remote Process Invocation – Request and Reply is the pattern: the scheduling system must confirm seat availability before responding, and the attendee needs to see success or "sold out" immediately, so Salesforce invokes the remote process and waits for its reply. Surge is handled by scaling and queueing in middleware, not by changing the pattern.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Remote Process Invocation – Fire and Forget) — discards the response the attendee is waiting for.
Option C (Batch Data Synchronization) — reconciles after the fact, so rooms could be overbooked in the meantime.
Option D (Remote Call-In) — the wrong direction: it describes an external system calling into Salesforce.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

question: Salesforce users need to read data from an external system via HTTPS request. Which two security methods should an integration architect leverage within Salesforce to secure the integration? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Connected App
optionB: Named Credentials
optionC: Authorization Provider
optionD: Two-way SSL
explanation:
Named Credentials (B) hold the endpoint plus the auth protocol — Basic, OAuth, JWT or mutual TLS — so Apex never handles secrets in code. Two-way SSL (D) authenticates client and server to each other with certificates, preventing impersonation in either direction.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Connected App) — configures inbound OAuth into Salesforce, not outbound consumption of someone else's service.
Option C (Authorization Provider) — a sub-component of an OAuth setup, used with a Named Credential rather than instead of one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_keys_uploading_mutual_auth_cert_api.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which two approaches will require the least amount of development effort when inserting leads from a source Salesforce org into a target Salesforce org? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Configure Named Credentials in the source org.
optionB: Use the Composite REST API to aggregate multiple leads in a single call.
optionC: Use the Tooling API with Process Builder to insert leads in real time.
optionD: Call the Salesforce REST API to insert the lead into the target system.
explanation:
Named Credentials (A) remove the hand-rolled OAuth and token-refresh code needed to authenticate against the target org. Composite REST (B) carries up to 25 subrequests in one call, cutting both API consumption and orchestration code.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Tooling API with Process Builder) — the Tooling API works on metadata, not record CRUD, so it cannot insert leads.
Option D (call the REST API per lead) — workable but the most effort: callout and auth code per record, with none of the consolidation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/resources_composite_composite_post.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters needs to make synchronous callouts to 'available to promise' services to query product availability and reserve inventory during the customer checkout process. Which two considerations should an integration architect make when building a scalable integration solution? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The typical and worst-case historical response times.
optionB: The number of batch jobs that can run concurrently.
optionC: How many concurrent service calls are being placed.
optionD: The maximum query cursors open per user on the service.
explanation:
The worst-case response time of the availability service (A) decides whether a synchronous callout at checkout is viable at all. Salesforce sets the Apex callout timeout to 10 seconds by default and setTimeout() raises it to 120, which is also the cumulative callout budget for one transaction — a budget to design against, not a fixed ceiling. Concurrent call volume (C) matters for the same reason: any synchronous request over 5 seconds counts against the org's concurrent long-running request limit, so checkout traffic can exhaust it even when each call succeeds.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (concurrent batch jobs) — batch Apex plays no part in a synchronous checkout flow.
Option D (query cursors per user) — a SOAP API paging concern, unrelated to reserving inventory.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2015/11/avoiding-the-concurrent-request-limit-via-synchronous-callout-optimization

corrected.note: Answer stands. The explanation described the 10-second callout timeout as a hard bound; it is the default, raisable to 120 seconds via setTimeout(), which is also the per-transaction cumulative limit. Restated so the sizing argument rests on the 120-second budget and the concurrent long-running request limit rather than on a ceiling that does not exist.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters is planning to perform nightly batch loads into Salesforce from an external system with a custom Java application using the Bulk API, and the CIO is curious about monitoring recommendations for the jobs from the Technical Architect. Which two recommendations will help meet the requirements? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Write the error response from the Bulk API status to a custom error-logging object in Salesforce using an Apex trigger, and create reports on the object.
optionB: Visually monitor in the Salesforce UI using 'Bulk Data Load Jobs' in the Setup menu.
optionC: Set the Salesforce debug log level to 'finest' and add the user ID running the job to monitor in the Debug Logs in the Setup menu.
optionD: Use the getBatchInfo method in the Java application to monitor the status of the jobs from the Java application.
explanation:
The "Bulk Data Load Jobs" page (B) is Salesforce's built-in monitor for job state, batch counts, records processed and failures, with no code. The Bulk API's getBatchInfo (D) lets the Java client poll batch status and react programmatically.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex trigger writing to a custom error log) — Bulk API failures are reported per job and batch, so a record trigger will not capture them reliably.
Option C (debug logs at "finest") — debug logs do not usefully cover Bulk API ingestion, and are not a monitoring strategy.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.monitoring_async_api_jobs.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_batches_monitor.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters wants to use Salesforce as a front end for creating accounts using the lead-to-opportunity process. (1) An order is created in Salesforce when the opportunity is closed/won, but the back-end ERP system is the data master for orders. (2) The customer wants to be able to see within Salesforce all the stages of order processing such as Order Created, Order Shipped, Order Paid, that are within the retention window. Which two message-durability considerations should an Integration Architect make when designing a solution to meet these business requirements? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: When subscribing to the Salesforce event bus, ReplayId is used with a value of -2 to be able to see old and new events.
optionB: High-volume event messages are stored for 24 hours (one day).
optionC: When subscribing to the Salesforce event bus, ReplayId is used with a value of -1 to be able to see new events.
optionD: High-volume event messages are stored for 72 hours (three days).
explanation:
ReplayId = -2 (A) starts a subscriber at the earliest event still in retention, which is what backfills order stage history after an outage. High-volume platform events are retained for 72 hours (D), which bounds how far back -2 can reach.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (stored for 24 hours) — not the current retention; the window is 72 hours.
Option C (ReplayId = -1) — delivers only events published after subscription, which defeats the durability requirement.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/pub-sub-api/guide/event-message-durability.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_subscribe_delivery.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) owns a variety of cloud-based applications, including Salesforce, alongside several on-premise applications. The on-premise applications are protected behind a corporate network with limited outside access to external systems. UC would like to expose data from the on-premise applications to Salesforce for a more unified user experience. The data should be accessible from Salesforce in real-time. Which two actions should be recommended to fulfill this system requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Develop an application in Heroku that connects to the on-premise database via an ODBC string and VPC connection.
optionB: Develop custom APIs on the company's network that are invokable by Salesforce.
optionC: Deploy MuleSoft to the on-premise network and design externally facing APIs to expose the data.
optionD: Run a batch job with an ETL tool from an on-premise server to move data to Salesforce.
explanation:
Real-time access into a locked-down network means exposing endpoints out of it: custom APIs published through a DMZ or reverse proxy (B), or MuleSoft deployed on-premise presenting externally addressable APIs with security, routing and policy built in (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Heroku over ODBC and a VPC connection) — still requires the on-premise database to be reachable from the cloud, which the stated constraint forbids.
Option D (ETL batch job) — moves data on a schedule, which contradicts the real-time requirement.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: A new Salesforce program has the following high-level abstract requirement: business processes executed on Salesforce require data updates between the internal systems and Salesforce. Which three relevant details should a Salesforce Integration Architect seek to specifically solve for integration architecture needs of the program? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Source and target system, directionality, data volume and transformation complexity, along with any middleware that can be leveraged.
optionB: Integration skills, SME availability, and program governance details.
optionC: Timing aspects — real-time/near real-time (synchronous or asynchronous), batch, update frequency.
optionD: Integration style — process based, data based, virtual integration.
optionE: Core functional and non-functional requirements for user experience design, encryption needs, community, and license choices.
explanation:
Integration architecture is shaped by the system pair, direction, volume and transformation needs (A), which drive pattern and middleware choice; by timing and latency (C), which decides synchronous against asynchronous; and by integration style (D) — process, data or virtual — which selects the pattern family.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (skills, SME availability, governance) — programme management concerns, not architecture inputs.
Option E (UX, encryption, community and license choices) — belong to the wider implementation rather than specifically to integration architecture.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: A company is planning on sending orders from Salesforce to a fulfillment system. The integration architect has been asked to plan for the integration. Which two questions should the integration architect consider? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Can the fulfillment system create new addresses within the Order Create service?
optionB: Can the fulfillment system make a callback into Salesforce?
optionC: Can the fulfillment system implement a contract-first Outbound Messaging interface?
optionD: Is the product catalog data identical at all times in both systems?
explanation:
Whether the fulfilment system can call back into Salesforce (B) decides whether status updates can be event-driven rather than polled. Whether it can implement Outbound Messaging's contract-first WSDL (C) decides whether the simplest declarative Fire-and-Forget option is available at all.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (create new addresses within the Order Create service) — business logic inside the service, not a question about how the two systems integrate.
Option D (identical product catalog at all times) — a master-data question; order integration does not require catalog parity.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--fire-and-forget
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An architect decided to use Platform Events for integrating Salesforce with an external system for a company. Which three things should an architect consider when proposing this type of integration mechanism? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: To subscribe to an event, the integration user in Salesforce needs Read access to the event entity.
optionB: Salesforce needs to be able to store information about the external system in order to know which event to send out.
optionC: The external system needs to have the same uptime in order to keep up with Salesforce Platform Events.
optionD: To publish an event, the integration user in Salesforce needs Create permission on the event entity.
optionE: Error handling must be performed by the remote service because the event is effectively handed off to the remote system for further processing.
explanation:
Platform Event entities respect object permissions: Read to subscribe (A) and Create to publish (D). Once published, Salesforce treats the event as delivered to the bus and does not retry per subscriber, so the subscriber owns retry and error semantics (E).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Salesforce stores information about the external system) — subscribers pull from the event bus, so Salesforce never needs the external system's address.
Option C (matched uptime) — unnecessary, because the 72-hour retention window is what covers a subscriber being down.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_subscribe.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_publish.htm

question: Service agents at Northern Trail Outfitters use Salesforce to manage cases and B2C Commerce for ordering. Which integration solution should an architect recommend in order for the service agents to see order history from a B2C Commerce system?
optionA: Salesforce B2C Commerce to Service Cloud Connector
optionB: A REST API offered by Commerce Platform
optionC: MuleSoft Anypoint Platform
optionD: REST API offered by Salesforce Platform
explanation:
The B2C Commerce to Service Cloud Connector is the pre-built Salesforce package that surfaces B2C order history, customer profile and order actions such as cancel and refund inside the Service Cloud console with minimal custom code.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Commerce Platform REST API) — rebuilds by hand what the Connector already ships.
Option C (MuleSoft Anypoint Platform) — adds a middleware tier and licence cost for a problem with a supported point solution.
Option D (Salesforce Platform REST API) — the wrong direction; it exposes Salesforce rather than retrieving Commerce order history.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.om_order_management_and_service_cloud.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/om-salesforce-order-management/om-connect-b2c-commerce-service-cloud

question: Northern Trail Outfitters submits orders to the manufacturing system web service. Recently, the system has experienced outages that kept service unavailable for several days. What solution should an architect recommend to handle errors during these types of service outages?
optionA: Use middleware queuing and buffering to insulate Salesforce from system outages.
optionB: Use Platform Event ReplayId and a custom scheduled Apex process to retrieve missed events.
optionC: Use @future jobId and a custom scheduled Apex process to retry failed service calls.
optionD: Use Outbound Messaging to automatically retry failed service calls.
explanation:
A middleware queue (A) holds order messages durably while the downstream is unavailable and replays them when it returns, so Salesforce never sees the outage and never burns governor limits retrying.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Platform Event ReplayId plus scheduled Apex) — only helps if the manufacturing system subscribes to Salesforce events, which is not this architecture.
Option C (@future jobId plus scheduled Apex retry) — consumes asynchronous Apex limits and loses context across an outage lasting days.
Option D (Outbound Messaging retries) — retries stop after 24 hours, well short of "several days".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--fire-and-forget

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a global financial company. UC support agents would like to open bank accounts on the spot for a customer who is inquiring about UC products. During the bank-account opening process, the agents execute credit checks for the customers through external agencies. At a given time, up to 30 concurrent agents will be using the service for performing credit checks for customers. What error-handling mechanism should be built to display an error to the agent when the credit verification process fails?
optionA: If the verification process is down, use a mock service to send the response to the agent.
optionB: Handle verification process errors in the Verification Web Service API in case there is a connection issue or the service responds with an error.
optionC: Handle integration errors in the middleware in case the verification process is down; the middleware should retry processing the request multiple times.
optionD: If the verification process is down, use a fire-and-forget mechanism instead of request-and-reply to allow the agent to get the response back when the service is back online.
explanation:
The agent needs an immediate and accurate error so they can retry or escalate in front of the customer. Handling connection failures and error responses at the callout and converting them into a visible message (B) is what produces that feedback.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (mock response when the service is down) — actively misleads the agent into believing a credit check ran.
Option C (silent middleware retries) — makes the agent wait on a failure that has already happened, with no signal.
Option D (switch to fire-and-forget) — abandons the synchronous answer the agent needs while the customer is present.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

question: An integration architect has been tasked with integrating Salesforce with an on-premises system. Due to established policies, this system must remain on-premises. What should the integration architect use to build a solution for this requirement?
optionA: Use Salesforce Connect if the database supports Open Database Connectivity (ODBC).
optionB: Use Heroku Connect if the data is hosted in Heroku.
optionC: Use Salesforce Connect if the database supports Open Data Protocol (OData).
explanation:
Salesforce Connect uses OData 2.0 or 4.0 to expose external data as external objects without copying it, which suits a source that must remain on-premise — typically fronted by an OData provider or the Salesforce Connect Secure Agent.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce Connect over ODBC) — Salesforce Connect does not consume ODBC; the adapter speaks OData.
Option B (Heroku Connect) — synchronises Heroku Postgres, which contradicts the requirement that the data stay on-premise.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect_odata.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An architect is required to integrate with an external data source via a Named Credential with an Apex callout due to technical constraints. How is authentication achieved?
optionA: Handle authentication with login flows.
optionB: Handle authentication in the code.
optionC: Connect via Salesforce Connect.
optionD: Connect via Communities.
explanation:
When an Apex callout references a Named Credential, the platform supplies the authentication header automatically from the credential's configured protocol — the Apex code does not assemble it, though the Apex callout is still the mechanism that carries it.
This item is poorly worded: the cleanest description is that the Named Credential handles authentication declaratively, and none of the four options says that.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (login flows) — govern how Salesforce users log in, not outbound callout authentication.
Option C (Salesforce Connect) — a separate external-object feature, and the stem specifies an Apex callout.
Option D (Communities) — a user-facing experience, unrelated to outbound authentication.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5

question: A large enterprise customer operating in a highly regulated industry is planning to implement Salesforce for customer-facing associates in both Sales and Service, and back-office staff. The business processes that Salesforce supports are critical to the business. Salesforce will be integrated to multiple back-office systems to provide a single interface for associates. Reliability and monitoring of these integrations are required as associates support customers. Which integration solution should the architect consider when planning the implementation?
optionA: Architect services in back-office systems to support callouts from Salesforce and build reliability, monitoring, and reporting capabilities.
optionB: Decouple back-office system callouts into separate distinct services that have inbuilt error-logging and monitoring frameworks.
optionC: Build a custom integration gateway to support back-office system integrations and ensure reliability and monitoring capabilities.
optionD: Leverage middleware for all back-office system integrations, ensuring real-time alerting, monitoring, and reporting capabilities.
explanation:
Middleware (D) is the right call in a regulated, mission-critical, multi-system landscape: routing, transformation, retry and circuit-breaking, audit logging and alerting all live in one place rather than being scattered across point-to-point callouts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (build the capabilities into each back-office service) — duplicates the work per system and produces inconsistent observability.
Option B (decouple into distinct services with their own logging) — better than nothing, but still gives operators no single pane of glass.
Option C (custom integration gateway) — hand-rolls what middleware already provides, and becomes a bespoke system to maintain.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: Which two requirements should the Salesforce Community Cloud support for self-registration and SSO? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: SAML SSO and Registration Handler
optionB: OpenID Connect Authentication Provider and Registration Handler
optionC: SAML SSO and Just-in-Time provisioning
optionD: OpenID Connect Authentication Provider and Just-in-Time provisioning
explanation:
Each protocol has its own auto-provisioning mechanism. OpenID Connect uses an Auth Provider plus a Registration Handler Apex class (B), which decides how the user record is created or matched. SAML uses Just-in-Time provisioning (C), driven by attribute mappings in the assertion.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SAML plus Registration Handler) — mixes the protocols: a Registration Handler belongs to an Auth Provider flow, not SAML.
Option D (OpenID Connect plus Just-in-Time provisioning) — the same mix-up in reverse; JIT is the SAML-side mechanism.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A large B2C customer is planning to implement Salesforce CRM to become a customer-centric enterprise. The goals for implementing Salesforce are: (1) develop a 360 view of customer; (2) leverage Salesforce capabilities for Marketing, Sales, and Service processes; (3) reuse enterprise capabilities built for Quoting and Order Management processes. Which three systems from the current system landscape can be retired with the implementation of Salesforce? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Order Management System
optionB: Case Management System
optionC: Sales Activity System
optionD: Email Marketing System
explanation:
Case management is replaced by Service Cloud (B), sales activity tracking by Sales Cloud (C) and email marketing by Marketing Cloud (D) — precisely the Marketing, Sales and Service capabilities the company wants natively.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Order Management System) — named in the requirements as an enterprise capability to be reused, so it stays.
Option E (Quoting System) — named the same way, and reuse is goal 3.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/sales-cloud-platform-quick-look
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/mrkt_cloud_basics

question: Northern Trail Outfitters wants to improve the quality of callouts from Salesforce to their REST APIs. For this purpose, they will require all API clients/consumers to adhere to REST API Markup Language (RAML) specifications that include field-level definition of every API request and response payload. RAML specs serve as interface contracts that Apex REST API clients can rely on. Which two design specifications should the Integration Architect include in the integration architecture to ensure that Apex REST API client unit tests confirm adherence to the RAML specs? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Call the Apex REST API clients in a test context to get the mock response.
optionB: Require the Apex REST API clients to implement the HttpCalloutMock interface.
optionC: Call the HttpCalloutMock implementation from the Apex REST API clients.
optionD: Implement HttpCalloutMock to return responses per RAML specification.
explanation:
An HttpCalloutMock implementation returning RAML-shaped responses (D) is what enforces the contract — the mock is the contract. Invoking the client in a test context with the mock registered (A) is what makes the framework substitute it at runtime.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (clients implement HttpCalloutMock) — the mock is a separate test class; a production client must not implement it.
Option C (clients call the mock implementation) — same error: the client never references the mock, the test wires it in.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing_httpcalloutmock.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is currently managing a custom monolithic web service that runs on an on-premise server. This monolithic web service is responsible for point-to-point integrations between (1) Salesforce and a legacy billing application, (2) Salesforce and a cloud-based ERP application, and (3) Salesforce and a data lake. UC has found that the tight interdependencies between systems are causing integrations to fail. What should an integration architect recommend to decouple the systems and improve the performance of the integrations?
optionA: Leverage modular design by breaking up the web service into smaller pieces for a microservice architecture.
optionB: Use the Salesforce Bulk API when integrating back into Salesforce.
optionC: Move the custom monolithic web service from on-premise to a cloud provider.
explanation:
Decoupling tightly interdependent integrations means decomposing the monolith into independently deployable services (A), each owning one integration concern and its own failure domain — which is what the cascading failures point to.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Bulk API for the return leg) — addresses data volume, a different problem from the coupling described.
Option C (move the monolith to a cloud provider) — changes where it runs while preserving every interdependency.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity

question: Universal Containers is planning to implement Salesforce as their CRM system. Currently they have the following systems: (1) Leads are managed in a Marketing System. (2) Salespeople use Microsoft Outlook to enter contacts, emails, and manage activities. (3) Inventory, Billing, and Payments are managed in their ERP system. The proposed CRM is expected to provide Sales and Support people the ability to have a single view of their customers and manage their contacts, emails, and activities in Salesforce CRM. What should an Integration Consultant consider to support the proposed CRM system strategy?
optionA: Plan for migration of customer and sales data across systems on a regular basis to keep them in sync.
optionB: Evaluate current and future data and system usage and then identify potential integration requirements to Salesforce.
optionC: Explore out-of-the-box Salesforce connectors for integration with ERP, Marketing, and Microsoft Outlook systems.
optionD: Propose a middleware system that can support interface between systems with Salesforce.
explanation:
The first step in a CRM programme with integrations is discovery: understanding current and projected data flows, volumes and usage (B), which is what then drives the technology choices.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (plan regular migration to keep systems in sync) — commits to an approach, and to ongoing duplication, before the requirements are known.
Option C (explore out-of-the-box connectors) — shopping for tools ahead of knowing what has to be integrated.
Option D (propose middleware) — may well be right eventually, but it is a solution chosen before the analysis.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: The director of customer service at Northern Trail Outfitters wants to capture and trend specific business events that occur in Salesforce in real time. The metrics will be accessed in an ad-hoc manner using an external analytics system. The events are: (1) a customer initiates a product exchange via a Case; (2) a customer service rep clicks on the 'Authorize Exchange Product' menu item in the Case; (3) a customer initiates a subscription cancellation via a Case; (4) a customer service rep clicks on the 'Initiate Refund' menu item in the Case. Which solution should meet these business requirements?
optionA: Case Workflow Rule that sends an Outbound Message
optionB: Case Trigger after insert, after update to publish the Platform Event
optionC: Case after-insert Trigger that executes a callout
explanation:
A Case Trigger on after insert and after update that publishes the Platform Event is the solution. Publishing from a trigger lets one piece of logic capture the record-state events (a case created, a status changed), while Apex published from the button handlers covers the UI-driven ones, and Platform Events are the canonical mechanism for real-time, ad-hoc subscription by an external analytics system.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Case Workflow Rule that sends an Outbound Message) — point-to-point SOAP with no fan-out, so it cannot feed ad-hoc subscribers, and it cannot capture a menu-item click.
Option C (Case after-insert Trigger that executes a callout) — couples Salesforce uptime to the analytics system, hits governor limits at scale, and fires only on insert, missing the status changes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_publish.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_subscribe.htm

question: A conglomerate is designing a Lightning Web Component (LWC) to display transactions aggregated from different sources. Their current system landscape is: (1) Transactions are created at any time through their various on-premise and cloud-based systems. (2) All necessary transactions are replicated to a custom Transaction object in Salesforce. It is updated periodically, so between updates it only has a subset of the necessary transactions. (3) Middleware supports publish-subscribe interactions and provides RESTful Enterprise APIs that can retrieve transactions from on-premise and cloud-based systems. The company wants to address a usability concern regarding incomplete data displayed on the LWC component. What should the Integration Architect specify so the LWC will be able to display all the required transactions?
optionA: Use the Continuation class to call the Enterprise APIs and then process the response in a callback method.
optionB: Publish a Platform Event, have the middleware subscribe and update the custom object on receipt of the Platform Event.
optionC: Let the Lightning Data Service with a wire adapter display new values when the custom object records change.
optionD: Call the Enterprise APIs directly from the LWC's JavaScript code and redisplay the LWC on receipt of the API response.
explanation:
The custom Transaction object is incomplete by design between syncs, so the component has to reach the middleware's Enterprise APIs at view time. Continuation (A) does exactly that: the callout runs asynchronously and resumes in a callback, releasing the application server thread, and it supports callouts up to 120 seconds. That matters because a synchronous request running over 5 seconds counts against the org's concurrent long-running request limit, which is what bites when many users open the component at once.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (publish a Platform Event for middleware to update the object) — still leaves a staleness window; the user sees whatever arrived before they looked.
Option C (Lightning Data Service with a wire adapter) — can only ever show what the partially populated custom object holds.
Option D (call the Enterprise APIs from LWC JavaScript) — pushes endpoint credentials and CSP configuration into the browser and bypasses Apex entirely.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_continuation_overview.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands at A. Carried forward from the earlier pass: the key was changed D->A because this question's twin answers Continuation for an identical stem and the deck contradicted itself. This pass additionally removed the phrase "hit the synchronous callout ceiling" — 10 seconds is the default Apex callout timeout, raisable to 120 seconds via setTimeout(), so the case for Continuation rests on releasing the request thread and on the concurrent long-running request limit, not on a ceiling that does not exist.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters uses a custom Java application to display code coverage and test results for all of their enterprise applications and is planning to include Salesforce as well. Which Salesforce API should an Integration Architect use to meet the requirement?
optionA: SOAP API
optionB: Analytics REST API
optionC: Metadata API
optionD: Tooling API
explanation:
Tooling API (D) exposes ApexCodeCoverage, ApexCodeCoverageAggregate, ApexTestResult and ApexTestRunResult — the entities a coverage and test dashboard needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (SOAP API) — works with records, and code coverage is not record data.
Option B (Analytics REST API) — serves CRM Analytics datasets, not Apex test telemetry.
Option C (Metadata API) — deploys and retrieves metadata but exposes no coverage results.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_tooling.meta/api_tooling/tooling_api_objects_apexcodecoverageaggregate.htm

question: A developer has been tasked by the integration architect to build a solution based on the Streaming API. The developer has done some research and has found there are different implementations of events in Salesforce (PushTopic Events, Change Data Capture, Generic Streaming, Platform Events), but is unsure of how to proceed with the implementation. The developer asks the system architect for some guidance. What should the architect consider when making the recommendation?
optionA: PushTopic Events can define a custom payload.
optionB: Change Data Capture does not have record access support.
optionC: Change Data Capture can be published from Apex.
optionD: Apex triggers can subscribe to Generic Events.
explanation:
Salesforce states that Change Data Capture ignores sharing settings and delivers change events for all records of an object, so "does not have record access support" (B) is true in as many words. Field-level security still applies: a subscriber receives every record's change but only the fields it may see.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (PushTopic Events can define a custom payload) — the weak point of this item, and worth an honest caveat: a PushTopic payload is shaped by its SOQL SELECT clause, so it is customisable in a limited sense. B is still the better answer, because "custom payload" describes generic streaming, where you post an arbitrary body, far better than choosing fields from one queried object.
Option C (CDC can be published from Apex) — false; change events are generated automatically from record changes.
Option D (Apex triggers can subscribe to Generic Events) — false; triggers can subscribe to platform events and change events, not generic events.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_security_considerations.htm

corrected.note: Q44 A->B. Salesforce documents that CDC ignores sharing settings and sends change events for all records, so "CDC does not have record access support" is the doc-backed true statement.

question: Which two system constraint questions should be considered when designing an integration to send orders from Salesforce to a fulfillment system? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: What latency is acceptable for orders to reach the fulfillment system?
optionB: Which system will validate order shipping addresses?
optionC: Can the fulfillment system implement a contract-first Outbound Messaging interface?
optionD: Can the fulfillment system participate in idempotent design to avoid duplicate orders?
explanation:
Acceptable latency (A) is a system constraint that selects synchronous against asynchronous and sizes any retry or queue. Idempotency support (D) is a constraint that decides whether at-least-once delivery is safe or whether the integration must deduplicate itself.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (which system validates shipping addresses) — business logic and ownership, not a system constraint.
Option C (can it implement contract-first Outbound Messaging) — a capability and implementation question; useful to ask, but it chooses a mechanism rather than describing a constraint.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a large printing company that sells advertisement banners. The company works with third-party agents on banner initial design concepts. The design files are stored in an on-premise file store that can be accessed by UC internal users and the third-party agencies. UC would like to collaborate with the third-party agencies on the design files and allow them to view the design files in the community. The conceptual design file size is 2.5 GB. Which solution should an integration architect recommend?
optionA: Create a Lightning component with a Request-and-Reply integration pattern to allow the community users to download the design files.
optionB: Define an External Data Source and use Salesforce Connect to upload the files to an external object. Link the external object using indirect lookup.
optionC: Create a custom object to store the file location URL; when a community user clicks on the file URL, redirect the user to the on-premise system file location.
optionD: Use Salesforce Files to link the files to Salesforce records and display the records and files in the community.
explanation:
The design files are mastered on-premise, and the practical answer is to leave them there: hold the file's location on a Salesforce record and redirect authorised community users to the on-premise store, so no 2.5 GB blob is copied, duplicated or kept in sync.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Request-and-Reply Lightning component) — streaming 2.5 GB through an Apex callout is not viable against heap and response-size limits.
Option B (External Data Source with Salesforce Connect) — surfaces external records as external objects; it does not serve arbitrary file blobs.
Option D (Salesforce Files) — note that size is not the reason. Salesforce Files accepts up to 10 GB in Files home, libraries and a record's Files list; the 2 GB figure applies only to Chatter posts, so 2.5 GB is within the limit. It fails because it copies the file into Salesforce at all, creating a second master and consuming storage for every revision.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=experience.collab_files_size_limits.htm&type=5

question: A global financial company sells financial products and services that include Bank Accounts, Loans, and Insurance. The company has a core banking system that is state of the art and is the master system to store financial transactions, financial products, and customer information. The core banking system currently processes 10 million financial transactions per day. The CTO is considering building a community portal so that customers can review their bank account details, update their information, and review their account financial transactions. What should an integration architect recommend as a solution to enable customer community users to view their financial transactions?
optionA: Use Salesforce Connect to display the financial transactions as an external object.
optionB: Replicate the financial transactions into Salesforce nightly using an ETL tool.
optionC: Use Salesforce External Services to display financial transactions in a community Lightning page.
optionD: Use an iframe to display core banking financial transactions data in the customer community.
explanation:
Salesforce Connect with an OData adapter surfaces the core banking transactions as external objects, so community users read live data with nothing copied into Salesforce — decisive when the source produces 10 million transactions a day and the bank must stay the system of record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (nightly ETL replication) — inflates storage, adds a day of lag and duplicates regulated financial data.
Option C (External Services) — invokes REST actions declaratively from Flow; it is not a way to browse a transaction list.
Option D (iframe the core banking UI) — sidesteps the platform's authentication and sharing model entirely.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect_odata.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a leading provider of management training globally. UC embarked on a Salesforce transformation journey to allow students to register for courses in the Salesforce community. UC has a learning system that masters all courses and student registration. UC requested a near real-time feed of student registration from Salesforce to the learning system. The integration architect recommends using a Salesforce Platform Event. Which API should be used for the Salesforce Platform Event solution?
optionA: Tooling API
optionB: Streaming API
optionC: REST API
optionD: SOAP API
explanation:
Streaming API over CometD is the channel an external subscriber uses to receive Platform Events as they are published.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Tooling API) — reaches metadata about the event definition, not the events themselves.
Option C (REST API) — synchronous record CRUD, with no way to subscribe to the event bus.
Option D (SOAP API) — the same limitation; it cannot subscribe either.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_subscribe.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has an integration set up between a Salesforce org and a quoting system. NTO would like to show a notification to all sales representatives that use Salesforce any time the quoting system will be taken down for maintenance. Which Salesforce API should an Integration Architect use to fulfill this requirement?
optionA: Connect REST API
optionB: Tooling API
optionC: REST API
optionD: Streaming API
explanation:
A real-time, fan-out "system going down" alert is what Streaming API and Platform Events deliver: the quoting system publishes a maintenance event and every subscribed Salesforce client receives it immediately, via empApi in the UI.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Connect REST API) — scoped to Chatter and communities, not a push channel for system alerts.
Option B (Tooling API) — metadata and developer tooling.
Option C (REST API) — synchronous request/response with no push semantics, so clients would have to poll.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_subscribe.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters is in the final stages of merging two Salesforce orgs but needs to keep the retiring org available for a short period of time for lead management, as it is connected to multiple public website forms. The sales department has requested that new leads are available in the new Salesforce instance within 30 minutes. Which two approaches will require the least amount of development effort? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Use the Tooling API with Process Builder to insert leads in real time.
optionB: Configure named credentials in the source org.
optionC: Call the Salesforce REST API to insert the lead into the target org.
optionD: Use the Composite REST API to aggregate multiple leads in a single call.
explanation:
Both orgs are Salesforce, so the retiring org needs only somewhere to authenticate and a way to move records. Named Credentials supply the target org's authentication declaratively, with no credential handling in code (B). Composite REST then carries many leads in one call — Salesforce documents it as reducing code and network overhead, with the whole series counting as a single API call, which matters when several web forms feed leads continuously against a 30-minute target (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Tooling API with Process Builder) — the Tooling API addresses metadata and developer tooling, not record CRUD.
Option C (call the REST API per lead) — works, but needs loop, batching and per-record error handling that Composite provides for free, so it is not the least effort.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/resources_composite_composite_post.htm

question: A security assessment of NTO's Salesforce orgs flagged unmanaged-package code that holds secrets — usernames, passwords, and OAuth tokens used for callouts — in plain text. Which persistence mechanisms should the integration architect require so secrets cannot be deliberately or accidentally exposed?
optionA: Encrypted Custom Fields and Protected Custom Settings
optionB: Named Credentials and Protected Custom Settings
optionC: Protected Custom Metadata Types and Named Credentials
explanation:
Named Credentials is Salesforce's recommended store for callout authentication: secrets are encrypted, never appear in debug logs, and the platform attaches the header itself. For secrets that must stay hidden even from admins or subscribers — the unmanaged-code case here — Protected Custom Metadata Types restrict access to Apex in the same namespace.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Encrypted Custom Fields and Protected Custom Settings) — encrypted fields are meant for PII such as SSNs, not for callout credentials.
Option B (Named Credentials and Protected Custom Settings) — the Named Credentials half is right, but Salesforce's guidance now favours Protected Custom Metadata over Custom Settings for deployability and packaging.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.secure_coding_guide.meta/secure_coding_guide/secure_coding_storing_sensitive_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5

question: NTO has had a surge of requests from other business units to share opportunity data, and developers have started writing asynchronous @future callouts directly into each target system. The CIO is worried about the long-term viability and scalability of this pattern. What should be done to address those concerns?
optionA: Refactor the @future methods to use Enhanced External Services, import Open API 2.0 schemas, and update Flows to call services instead of Apex.
optionB: Implement an extract, transform, load (ETL) tool and run nightly batch loads to reduce network traffic.
optionC: Implement an Enterprise Service Bus for orchestration, mediation, and routing, and decouple Salesforce from each downstream system.
explanation:
@future callouts wired directly into each target system produce a point-to-point tangle in which Salesforce owns every endpoint, auth scheme and error path — the viability and scaling risk the CIO is naming. An ESB centralises routing, transformation and quality of service, so a downstream change touches only the ESB.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Enhanced External Services with Open API schemas) — tidier than @future, but still point-to-point: Salesforce keeps owning every endpoint.
Option B (nightly ETL batch loads) — defeats the near-real-time intent the existing callouts were built for.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity

question: An enterprise customer is implementing Salesforce specifically to support case management. Their current landscape has an Email Management System, an Order Management System, a Case Management System, and a Data Warehouse that feeds a downstream Analytics/BI tool. Considering Salesforce's native case management capabilities, which three systems should the integration architect plan to integrate Salesforce with?
optionA: Order Management System, Data Warehouse, and Case Management System
optionB: Email Management System, Order Management System, and Case Management System
optionC: Data Warehouse, Order Management System, and Email Management System
explanation:
Service Cloud replaces the legacy Case Management System, so it is retired rather than integrated. The other three each have a purpose: Email Management feeds inbound messages so they create and update cases, the Order Management System gives agents context in the console, and the Data Warehouse receives case data for the downstream BI tool.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Order Management, Data Warehouse, Case Management) — keeps the redundant Case Management System and drops Email Management.
Option B (Email Management, Order Management, Case Management) — keeps the redundant Case Management System and drops the Data Warehouse the BI tool depends on.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.om_order_management_and_service_cloud.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: NTO is setting up Salesforce Connect against an external data source that supports OData. Which configuration should the integration architect use to secure requests originating from Salesforce?
optionA: Configure Identity Type for the OData connection.
optionB: Configure a certificate for the OData connection.
optionC: Configure Special Compatibility for the OData connection.
explanation:
Identity Type is the Salesforce Connect setting that decides how requests authenticate outward: Named Principal uses one shared service account for everyone, while Per User makes each Salesforce user supply their own credentials and respects that user's permissions in the source system. That is the authorisation boundary.
