Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (configure a certificate) — helps with transport-layer security, but it is not the request-authorisation control being asked about.
Option C (Special Compatibility) — exists to accommodate non-standard OData providers, not to secure anything.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.platform_connect_identity_type.htm&type=5

question: A training provider must verify every third-party trainer through 10 different accreditation agencies before that trainer can deliver courses. Each agency responds on its own schedule and the full verification can take days. The company wants to automate this by integrating with each agency's web service. What is the recommended approach?
optionA: Make an Apex callout from an @future method to all 10 agencies in parallel.
optionB: Use middleware to call the 10 verification services, consolidate the results, then call back into Salesforce to set the trainer's status to 'verified.'
optionC: Use Salesforce External Services to make the callouts and continue polling each agency until every result is verified, then update the trainer.
explanation:
A multi-day, multi-system orchestration with asynchronous callbacks is beyond what Salesforce holds open: Apex transactions cap at 120 seconds. Middleware fans out to the ten agencies, holds state until every one responds — over days if needed — then makes a single remote call-in to set the trainer's status.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (@future callouts to all ten in parallel) — carries the same transaction cap, so it cannot wait days, and it burns asynchronous Apex limits.
Option C (External Services with polling) — External Services drives declarative, synchronous Flow actions and cannot manage a multi-day waiting state.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm

question: NTO's corporate security guidelines now require all cloud applications to pass through a secure firewall before they reach on-premise resources. The team is evaluating middleware products. Which capability should the integration architect prioritize when choosing one?
optionA: The middleware can interface directly with on-premise databases via an ODBC connection string.
optionB: The middleware enforces the OAuth security protocol.
optionC: The middleware can establish a secure API gateway between cloud applications and on-premise resources.
explanation:
A firewall-protected entry point for cloud traffic needs a component that can sit in the DMZ and terminate inbound TLS — the API gateway role. That is what enables IP allow-listing of Salesforce ranges, mutual TLS and rate limiting before a request reaches anything internal.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (direct ODBC connection string to on-premise databases) — exposing a database protocol through a cloud-facing firewall is the anti-pattern the guideline exists to prevent.
Option B (enforces OAuth) — an authorisation protocol, useful but not a network perimeter; it does not satisfy the requirement on its own.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: A customer is migrating from a legacy system to Salesforce and wants to integrate every system that currently works with the legacy application. Which constraint should the integration architect weigh most heavily when choosing the integration pattern?
optionA: Multi-language and multi-currency requirements
optionB: Data volume and processing volume
optionC: Reporting and usability requirements
explanation:
Salesforce is multi-tenant with strict governor limits, and volume drives pattern selection more than anything else: large data sets force Bulk API over REST or SOAP, high processing volume forces asynchronous patterns over synchronous request/reply, and large read-only sets often belong in Salesforce Connect rather than stored at all.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (multi-language and multi-currency) — functional configuration that does not change the integration plumbing.
Option C (reporting and usability) — shapes what users see, not which integration pattern the data has to travel through.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: Universal Containers is decommissioning its legacy CRM and migrating data into Salesforce. The data migration team has asked for a recommendation that will optimize the performance of the load. Which approach should the integration architect recommend?
optionA: Use the Bulk API to process jobs in parallel mode.
optionB: Use the Bulk API to process jobs in serial mode.
optionC: Contact Salesforce Support to schedule a performance load.
explanation:
Bulk API in parallel mode lets Salesforce process several batches of the same job at once, which is the fastest route through a migration window. The standard guardrail is to sort the input by parent ID so batches do not contend for the same parent records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (serial mode) — processes one batch at a time and exists to dodge row-lock contention, so it is slower by design.
Option C (schedule a load with Salesforce Support) — reserved for genuinely extreme volumes, not a standard migration.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: A customer loads data into Salesforce with the Bulk API using a batch size of 2,000 in parallel mode, and the batches fail frequently with 'Max CPU time exceeded.' Reducing the batch size will fix the error. What should the architect call out as the trade-off of using a smaller batch size?
optionA: Smaller batch size can trigger 'Too many concurrent batches' errors.
optionB: Smaller batch size may exceed the concurrent API request limits.
optionC: Smaller batch size may increase the time required to execute the bulk job.
explanation:
A smaller batch processes fewer records per transaction, which keeps CPU time under the per-transaction limit but multiplies the number of batches for the same data set. Each batch carries fixed initialisation and finalisation overhead, so the job takes longer overall — the trade-off the team will actually feel. The daily Bulk API batch allocation, around 15,000 per 24 hours, is worth knowing alongside it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A ("Too many concurrent batches") — governed by parallel-mode scheduling, not by how large each batch is.
Option B (exceeding concurrent API request limits) — also a concurrency concern rather than a consequence of batch size.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2014/08/managing-task-locks-data-loads

question: Universal Containers wishes to validate street addresses in Salesforce against their legacy Accounting system, which is the system of record. Retrieving an Account record in this system takes 7-12 seconds per query, and the address must be validated as quickly as possible to ensure proper order processing. What integration pattern should an Architect suggest?
optionA: Outbound Message with a Callback.
optionB: Nightly batch validating records modified the previous day.
optionC: @Future method with an Apex callout.
optionD: Remote Invocation initiated by Middleware
explanation:
An Apex callout has no 10-second ceiling: 10 seconds is the default timeout and HttpRequest.setTimeout() raises it to as much as 120, which is also the cumulative callout budget for a transaction. So a 7–12 second lookup is not blocked by a limit — it is blocked by what the wait costs. Holding a user-facing transaction open on every address save is unacceptable latency and spends most of the callout budget on one query. Outbound Messaging with a callback takes the wait off the user's path: Salesforce sends the message on save, the accounting system validates at its own pace and the callback writes the result back, with the platform retrying for up to 24 hours.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (nightly batch of yesterday's changes) — far too slow for "as quickly as possible", and orders would process against unvalidated addresses all day.
Option C (@future method with a callout) — asynchronous, but with no delivery guarantee and no callback contract to return the result to the record.
Option D (Remote Invocation initiated by middleware) — inverts the trigger: the legacy system would have to know when a Salesforce address needed checking.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000232687&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: The explanation asserted a "10-second synchronous Apex callout ceiling". Salesforce documents 10 seconds as the default callout timeout, adjustable via setTimeout() up to 120 seconds (also the per-transaction cumulative limit), so no platform ceiling is crossed at 7-12 seconds. The answer is unchanged — Outbound Messaging still wins — but it wins on latency and delivery guarantees rather than on a limit that does not exist.

question: A large enterprise customer with the following system landscape is planning to implement Salesforce Sales Cloud. The following business processes need to be supported in Salesforce: 1. Sales Consultants should be able to have access to current inventory. 2. Enterprise Resource Planning System(ERP) is the system of record for pricing information. 3. Quotes should be generated in Salesforce with pricing from ERP. 4. Sales Management uses a Enterprise Business Intelligence (BI) tool to view Sales dashboards. 5. Master Data Management (MDM) is the system of record for customers and prospects. 6. Invoices should be accessible in Salesforce. Which systems in the landscape should the Integration Consultant consider to be integrated with Salesforce to support the business requirements?
optionA: ERP, MDM, Data Warehouse, Invoices system
optionB: ERP, Inventory, Pricing Engine, Invoices system
optionC: ERP, MDM, BI tool and Data Warehouse
optionD: ERP, Invoices system, Data Warehouse and BI Tool
explanation:
Requirement 5 makes the MDM the system of record for customers and prospects, so Salesforce cannot own that data and the MDM must be integrated. Option A covers the ERP (pricing for quotes, and the inventory consultants need), the MDM, the Invoices system for requirement 6, and the Data Warehouse that feeds the BI dashboards in requirement 4.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (ERP, Inventory, Pricing Engine, Invoices) — drops the MDM entirely and invents a standalone Pricing Engine, when requirement 2 names the ERP as the pricing system of record.
Option C (ERP, MDM, BI tool, Data Warehouse) — omits the Invoices system that requirement 6 asks for, and integrating the BI tool directly is redundant when the Data Warehouse already feeds it.
Option D (ERP, Invoices, Data Warehouse, BI tool) — omits the MDM, so the customer master has no source.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

corrected.note: Q62 B->A. Requirement 5 names MDM as system of record for customers; option B omits it and invents a Pricing Engine.

question: KiA B2C Enterprise Customer has the following use case that involves processing payment from an external payment gateway service in Salesforce. 1. Customer requests Customer Service Representative (CSR) for a Service upgrade. 2. Customer provides credit card details to CSR for payment. 3. CSR submits payment information in Salesforce, and processed in a 4. CSR receives confirmation of payment. 5. CSR upgrades service for customer and confirms Customer. external payment gateway. This use case requires the CSR to obtain confirmation of payment before upgrading the service. The integration with Payment gateway needs to be reliable and monitored for audit purposes. The payment gateway service is an external RESTful service that the B2C Enterprise Customer has subscribed for. What should an Integration Architect recommend for this integration?
optionA: Make a callout to the payment gateway through ESB supporting error handling andlogging for audit purposes.
optionB: Platform events allow integration to payment gateway through the exchange ofreal-time event data, platform events are scalable and secure.
optionC: Use External Services feature to integrate gateway to Salesforce ensuring real-timeupdates the CSR and support post payment processes.
optionD: Build a custom Apex Callout to external Payment gateway service and provide success message to the CSR, the details of calloutsand responses are logged for audit purposes.
explanation:
This is a synchronous, business-critical payment that has to be reliable and auditable. Routing the callout through an ESB centralises error handling, logging, retries and monitoring, and still returns the confirmation the CSR must see before upgrading the service.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Platform Events) — asynchronous, so it cannot return the payment confirmation the CSR is waiting on.
Option C (External Services) — declarative and convenient, but it supplies no robust audit or error-handling layer for a payment.
Option D (custom Apex callout with logging) — workable, but every retry, audit and monitoring capability is hand-built and lives in one org rather than in a managed integration tier.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

question: Universal Containers (UC) has an existing web-based application that a group of employees use on a regular basis. These employees often have Salesforce and the web-based application open and find themselves manually moving the data between both. UC would like the two systems to be integrated so that the employees will see all the data in one screen without the need for manually updating the data. What integration pattern can help accomplish this requirement?
optionA: Use the Force.com canvas framework to embed the external application into Salesforce.
optionB: Use Rest API to pull data from Salesforce and update the external application.
optionC: Use Steaming API to create a push topic to send the message to the external system asynchronously.
explanation:
The requirement is to show an external application's data inside Salesforce on one screen without re-keying. The Canvas framework is built to embed an external web app in the Salesforce UI, passing signed context and authentication with it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (REST API to pull data and update the external app) — moves data between the systems but still leaves the employee looking at two applications.
Option C (Streaming API push topic) — sends change notifications asynchronously; it delivers no unified screen either.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_connect.meta/platform_connect/canvas_framework_intro.htm

question: Universal containers has complex data transformation, error handling and process automation requirements as part of their integration strategy. What technology should an Architect recommend in order to minimize Salesforce code customizations?
optionA: Middleware
optionB: Data Loader
optionC: Canvas
optionD: Process Builder
explanation:
Complex transformation, error handling and cross-system process automation are middleware responsibilities. Putting them in an ETL or ESB tier keeps the logic off-platform and minimises custom Apex, which is what the question optimises for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Data Loader) — moves data in and out; it transforms nothing and automates no process.
Option C (Canvas) — embeds an external UI inside Salesforce and has no bearing on data transformation.
Option D (Process Builder) — runs inside Salesforce, so it increases platform customisation rather than reducing it.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity

question: Universal Containers would like to use a hard-coded username/password/security token of a user with a System Administrator profile to integrate its back-end system to Salesforce for inbound API calls. Which two security issues are associated with this approach.
optionA: Unintended password resets will cause the integration to stop working and disrupt business processes.
optionB: Unsecure storage of the credentials may result in hackers gaining unauthorized access to Salesforce.
optionC: Apex web services can executive with system privileges with such Salesforce credentials.
optionD: All back-end systems get uncontrolled access to any data within the Salesforce environment.
explanation:
The question asks specifically for security issues. Credentials that must be stored somewhere to be replayed are exposed to anyone who can read that store, and an attacker who obtains them inherits a System Administrator session (B). Because the profile is System Administrator, every back-end system using it reaches all data rather than the narrow slice it needs (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (unintended password resets break the integration) — a genuine risk, but an availability and continuity problem: a reset stops the integration, it exposes nothing.
Option C (Apex web services can execute with system privileges) — describes normal platform behaviour rather than a flaw introduced by this approach.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.secure_coding_guide.meta/secure_coding_guide/secure_coding_storing_sensitive_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5

question: A customer's enterprise architect has identified requirements around caching, queuing, error handling, alerts, retries, event handling, etc. The company has asked the Salesforce integration architect to help fulfill such aspects with their Salesforce program. Which three recommendations should the Salesforce integration architect make? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Transform a fire-and-forget mechanism to request-reply should be handled bymiddleware tools (like ETL/ESB) to improve performance.
optionB: Event handling processes such as writing to a log, sending an error or recovery process, or sending an extra message, can be assumed to be handled by middleware.
optionC: Event handling in a publish/subscribe scenario, the middleware can be used to route requests or messages to active data-event subscribers from active data-event publishers.
optionD: Message transformation and protocol translation should be done within Salesforce. Recommend leveraging Salesforce native protocol conversion capabilities as middle watools are NOT suited for such tasks
optionE: Provide true message queueing for integration scenarios (including orchestration,process choreography, quality of service, etc.) given that a middleware solution is required.
explanation:
Caching, queuing, error handling, alerts, retries and event handling are classic middleware responsibilities. Middleware should own event-handling side effects such as logging and recovery (B), broker publish/subscribe routing between publishers and subscribers (C), and provide true message queuing with orchestration and quality of service (E).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (convert fire-and-forget to request-reply for performance) — not a general recommendation; forcing a synchronous reply usually costs performance rather than improving it.
Option D (do transformation and protocol translation inside Salesforce) — inverts the advice. That work belongs in middleware, and the claim that middleware is unsuited to it is false.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses Salesforce to create and manager accounts and opportunities. With Salesforce being the master of records, the opportunities on existing accounts are required to be updated with product usage statistics from an on-premise usage tracking system that is capable of participating in contract-first integration. Which three steps should the Integration Architect consider given that UC does not want any custom development in Salesforce?
optionA: Use a REST API callback to update the Opportunity record with the product usage data from the remote system.
optionB: Generate a partner WSDL in Salesforce and provide it to the remote system to create a client stub.
optionC: Create a Workflow outbound message during Opportunity creation and provide the Opportunity ID and Session ID to the remote system.
optionD: Use a SOAP API callback to update the Opportunity record with the product usage data from the remote system.
optionE: Create a Process Builder outbound message during Opportunity creation and provide the Opportunity ID and Session ID to the remote system.
explanation:
With Salesforce as master and no custom development allowed, the design is contract-first. Generate the partner WSDL so the remote system can build a client stub against a loosely typed schema that survives metadata changes (B). Use a declarative Workflow outbound message on Opportunity creation to push the Opportunity Id (C) — configured entirely in Setup, no Apex. The remote system then makes a SOAP API callback to write the usage data onto the Opportunity (D).
One detail of option C is now out of date: Salesforce removed the session ID from outbound messages in February 2026, so the Send Session ID checkbox is gone, IncludeSessionId is always FALSE and no sessionID element is sent. The pattern is unchanged and the answer still stands, but a remote system built today must authenticate its callback with OAuth 2.0 instead.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (REST API callback) — a custom REST callback needs exactly the Apex development the question rules out.
Option E (Process Builder outbound message) — Process Builder cannot send outbound messages; that action belongs to flows, workflow rules, approval processes and entitlement processes.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005232763&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_partner.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands at B,C,D. Flagged because option C describes sending a Session ID in an outbound message, a mechanism Salesforce removed in February 2026 — the Send Session ID checkbox is gone, IncludeSessionId is forced to FALSE, and the sessionID element is no longer emitted. The pattern is unaffected, but the callback must now authenticate with OAuth 2.0, so the explanation says so rather than teaching a retired capability.

question: A customer imports data from an external system into Salesforce using Bulk API. These jobs have batch sizes of 2000 and are run in parallel mode. The batc fails frequently with the error "Max CPU time exceeded". A smaller batch size will fix this error. Which two options should be considered when using a smaller batch size? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Smaller batch size may cause record-locking errors.
optionB: Smaller batch size may increase time required to execute bulk jobs.
optionC: Smaller batch size can trigger "Too many concurrent batches" error.
optionD: Smaller batch size may exceed the concurrent API request limits.
explanation:
Reducing the batch size relieves "Max CPU time exceeded" because fewer records are processed per transaction, but it carries two costs. The first is locking: batch size does not cause contention by itself, but cutting it spreads the same records over more batches, so with unsorted data a parent's child records are likelier to straddle batches running at the same time (A). The documented remedy is to group records by parent within a batch, or to run in serial mode. The second is time — the same volume across more batches, each with its own start-up and finalisation overhead, takes longer end to end (B).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C ("Too many concurrent batches") — governed by parallel-mode scheduling, not by how many records a batch holds.
Option D (exceeding concurrent API request limits) — also a concurrency limit, unaffected by batch size.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2014/08/managing-task-locks-data-loads
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

corrected.note: Answer confirmed, mechanism made precise. Salesforce documents that lock contention comes from detail records sharing a parent being loaded in separate parallel batches, not from batch size as such; a smaller batch raises the risk only because it spreads a parent's children across more concurrent batches. The remedy is grouping by parent or serial mode.

question: Universal Containers send quotes to customers periodically when the customer contract is near expiration. Quoting is generated by an external quoting engine. The VP recommends that the quote-generated request should be sent one week prior to the contract expiration. The Quote engine requires the latest account, contact, and contract information from Salesforce to generate the quote. What is the recommended solution?
optionA: Workflow-initiated outbound message with a callback to gather additional information from Salesforce.
optionB: A scheduled batch Apex to gather additional information from Salesforce and make a sync callout to the quote engine.
optionC: Workflow-initiated alert to the Sales Rep, who will submit a request from a custom controller in a Visualforce page.
optionD: Workflow-initiated Apex to gather additional information from Salesforce and make a sync callout to the quote engine.
explanation:
The request has to fire on a schedule — one week before contract expiration — and assemble related account, contact and contract data, so a scheduled Batch Apex job that queries the data and makes a synchronous callout to the quoting engine fits cleanly.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (workflow-initiated outbound message with a callback) — outbound messaging is not time-based, and the callback adds a round trip to gather data the job could have queried itself.
Option C (workflow alert to the rep, who submits from a Visualforce page) — makes a scheduled, automatic process depend on a human remembering to click.
Option D (workflow-initiated Apex with a synchronous callout) — workflow fires on record change, not one week before a date, so the timing requirement is unmet.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: A call center manager uses a custom dashboard to track Case related metrics. The manager wants a component to display the number of closed Cases in real time. What type of event should be used to meet this requirement?
optionA: Push Topic Event
optionB: Change Data Capture Event
optionC: Platform Event
optionD: Generic Event
explanation:
A Push Topic Event is the right type. A Push Topic is defined by a SOQL query, so it watches precisely the records that matter — closed Cases — and notifies the dashboard component as records begin to match, which is the shape of this requirement. One caveat: Salesforce now labels Push Topic events legacy and steers new work elsewhere, so the real-world answer is drifting even though this remains the intended one.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Change Data Capture Event) — would surface the same changes, but it emits every change on the object with no query criteria, leaving the component to filter the stream. It is built for replicating records to an external store rather than driving a UI counter, which is why this item and the LMS-synchronisation item resolve in opposite directions.
Option C (Platform Event) — a custom message channel that no record change raises; something would have to publish it.
Option D (Generic Event) — the same, with an arbitrary payload and no record context at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_streaming.meta/api_streaming/pushtopic_events_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_intro.htm

corrected.note: Reviewed against the comment suggesting Change Data Capture. The answer stands: this asks for a query-scoped counter feeding a dashboard, which is what PushTopic is for. Note the opposite call on Q93, deliberately — CDC there, PushTopic here.

question: When user clicks Check Preferences as part of a Lightning flow in Salesforce, preferences from an externally hosted RESTful service are to be checked in real-time. The RESTful service has OpenAPI 2.0 JSON definitions, responding in data types of Boolean and string values. Which integration pattern and mechanism should be selected to meet the conditions?
optionA: Fire and Forget: Process-driven platform events publishes events on Salesforce Event Bus.
optionB: Remote Call-In: Salesforce REST API with REST Composite Resources.
optionC: Request-Reply: Enhanced External Services invokes a REST API.
optionD: Data Virtualization: Salesforce Connect map data external REST data in external objects.
explanation:
Calling an externally hosted REST service in real time from a Lightning flow, where the service is described by an OpenAPI definition, is the Request-Reply case Enhanced External Services is built for: it imports the schema and generates invocable actions usable directly in Flow.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Fire and Forget with platform events) — returns no synchronous reply, so the flow cannot show the preference it just asked for.
Option B (Remote Call-In with REST Composite) — describes an external system calling into Salesforce, the opposite direction.
Option D (Data Virtualization with Salesforce Connect) — maps external data as external objects for browsing, rather than invoking a service action and reading its Boolean and string reply.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.external_services.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

question: Universal Containers (UC) has multiple orgs with Sales and Service Cloud implementation to support different lines of business. UC is planning to consolidate Salesforce orgs to benefit from a 360-degree view of the customer based on revenue, support requests, and contracts. What should an Architect recommend?
optionA: Use a custom REST service for data cleaning and standardization.
optionB: Use a custom SOAP service for data cleaning and standardization.
optionC: Use standard SOAP API for data cleaning and standardization.
optionD: Use staging tables with an ETL tool for data cleaning and standardization.
explanation:
Consolidating orgs for a 360-degree view means merging, de-duplicating, cleaning and standardising large volumes, which belongs in staging tables and an ETL tool outside Salesforce.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom REST service) — moves data but supplies no matching, cleansing or transformation, and is code to maintain.
Option B (custom SOAP service) — the same gap in a different protocol.
Option C (standard SOAP API) — a transport for records; it performs none of the de-duplication a consolidation needs.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: Given the diagram below, a Salesforce org, middleware, and Historical data store (with 20million records and growing) exists with connectivity between them Historical records are archived from Salesforce and moved to Historical Data store (which houses 20M records and growing; fine-tuned to be performant with search queries). Call center agents use Salesforce, when reviewing occasional special cases, have requested access to view the related historical case items that relate to submit cases. Which mechanism and patterns are recommended to maximize declarative configuration?
optionA: C Use an ESB tool with a fire and forget pattern and then publish a platform event for the requested historical data.
optionB: Use an ESB tool with Request-Reply pattern and then make a real-time Apex callout to the ESB endpoint to fetch and display component related to Case object
optionC: Use ESB tool with Data Virtualization pattern, expose OData endpoint, and then use Salesforce Connect to consume and display the External Object alongside with the Caseobject.
optionD: Use an ETL tool with a Batch Data Synchronization pattern to migrate historical data into Salesforce and into a custom object (historical data) related to Case object.
explanation:
Exposing 20 million and growing historical records for occasional viewing, with maximum declarative configuration, is the Data Virtualization pattern: the ESB exposes an OData endpoint and Salesforce Connect consumes it as an external object displayed alongside the Case.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ESB fire-and-forget, then publish a platform event) — asynchronous and returns nothing for the agent to look at when they open the case.
Option B (ESB Request-Reply with a real-time Apex callout) — would work, but requires the Apex development the question asks to minimise.
Option D (ETL batch synchronisation into a custom object) — copies 20 million growing records into Salesforce, the outcome virtualisation exists to avoid.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect_odata.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is building a native mobile application that queries and updates data in their Salesforce in real time. What statement is correct about the Salesforce APIs?
optionA: Rest API supports oAuth
optionB: Enterprise WSDL minimizes payload size.
optionC: Enterprise WSDL supports WS-Security
optionD: REST API supports WS-Security.
explanation:
For a native mobile app reading and updating Salesforce in real time, the correct factual statement is that the REST API supports OAuth — the standard lightweight authentication for mobile clients.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Enterprise WSDL minimizes payload size) — the reverse: it is strongly typed and verbose, and SOAP envelopes are heavier than REST JSON.
Option C (Enterprise WSDL supports WS-Security) — Salesforce's SOAP APIs authenticate with a session ID or OAuth, not the WS-Security header.
Option D (REST API supports WS-Security) — WS-Security is a SOAP specification and has no meaning for REST.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/intro_understanding_authentication.htm

question: Universal Container needs to integrate Salesforce with several home-grown systems. These systems require custom code to be written in order to integrate with them, and the CIO argues that if custom code needs to be written, then there is no reason to invest in middleware. Which three considerations should an Architect bring up to the CIO? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Bulkification
optionB: Performance
optionC: Logging
optionD: Orchestration
explanation:
Even when custom code is needed to reach home-grown systems, middleware still adds value the CIO should weigh: centralised logging (C), orchestration of multi-step and multi-system processes (D), and consistent error handling and retry (E).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Bulkification) — a property of the integration code itself, which you write either way; middleware does not supply it.
Option B (Performance) — likewise addressed inside the integration, and adding a middleware hop generally costs a little latency rather than saving it, so it is not the argument to make.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/application-networks-and-api-led-connectivity-in-mulesoft/explore-api-led-connectivity

question: Universal Containers is a global financial company that sells financial products and services including, bank accounts, loans, and insurance. UC uses Salesforce Service cloud to service their customer via calls, live chat. The support agents would open bank accounts on the spot for customers who are inquiring about UC bank accounts. UC Core banking system is the system of record for bank accounts and all accounts opened in salesforce have to be synced in real-time to the core banking system. Support agents need to inform the customers with the newly created bank account ID which has to be generated from the core banking system. Which integration pattern is recommended for this use case?
optionA: Use request and reply.
optionB: Use salesforce platform event.
optionC: Use streaming API to generate push topic.
optionD: Use outbound message.
explanation:
The agent must receive the externally generated bank account Id before continuing the conversation, so the interaction has to be synchronous — the Request-and-Reply pattern.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Platform Event) — asynchronous, so the generated Id never comes back to the waiting agent.
Option C (Streaming API push topic) — pushes notifications about Salesforce records outward; it does not call the core banking system or return an Id.
Option D (Outbound message) — fire-and-forget SOAP with no synchronous reply.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

question: Universal Containers is building a mobile application that connects to Salesforce for reading and updating data. What is the appropriate authentication solution?
optionA: Prompt for the mobile user's username and password; utilize the Enterprise WSDL login() operation to obtain a session ID.
optionB: Prompt for the mobile user's username and Password; utilize the oAuth Username-Password flow to obtain an oAuth token.
optionC: Create a mobile Integration user ID whose credentials are stored within the mobile application code.
optionD: Redirect to Salesforce via the User-agent oAuth flow to obtain an access token and refresh token.
explanation:
Of the four, only the User-Agent OAuth flow keeps the user's password out of the app: the app redirects to Salesforce, the user authenticates there, and the app receives an access token and a refresh token.
Worth knowing beyond this question: Salesforce now recommends the OAuth 2.0 web server flow with PKCE instead, and admins can block apps using the user-agent flow, which returns the token in the redirect URL where other apps on the device may observe it. D remains the best answer here only because no option offers web server plus PKCE.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (username and password to the SOAP login() call) — the app handles the raw credentials and stores a session ID, with no refresh mechanism.
Option B (OAuth Username-Password flow) — nominally OAuth, but the app still collects and transmits the password, losing the point of the redirect.
Option C (shared integration user credentials in app code) — the worst of the four: one identity for every user, embedded where it can be extracted from the binary.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.remoteaccess_oauth_user_agent_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer stands at D — it is the best of the options offered. Flagged because Salesforce's current guidance is explicit that the web server flow with PKCE should be used instead of the user-agent flow, which uses the implicit grant and can expose the access token in the redirect URL. The explanation now says so rather than presenting the user-agent flow as the recommended mobile pattern.

question: A customer is migrating from an old legacy system to Salesforce. As part of the modernization effort, they would like to integrate al existing systems that currently work with their legacy application with Salesforce. Which three constraints and pain-points should an integration architect consider when choosing the integration pattern/mechanism? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Error handling mechanisms
optionB: Data Volume and Processing volume
optionC: System types - APIs, File systems, Email
optionD: Multi-language and multi-currency requirement
explanation:
Choosing a pattern when modernising off a legacy platform turns on the error-handling each interface needs (A), the data and processing volumes involved (B), and the variety of system and interface types you must meet — APIs, file systems, email (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option D (multi-language and multi-currency) — application configuration; it does not change which integration mechanism you choose.
Option E (reporting and usability) — shapes the user experience rather than the integration plumbing.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has Wave Analytics in their Salesforce org. UC has expertise and access to the Dell boomi ETL tool. UC would like to get all leads and opportunities from the org and data from a few other Marketing tools to a Wave instance for enhanced analysis. What is the recommended solution to set up the data process?
optionA: Use Wave data flow for Salesforce data and data from other sources.
optionB: Wave Data flow for Salesforce data and Dell boomi for data from other sources.
optionC: Export data from all sources into Excel and use Wave connector to import data.
optionD: Dell boomi for data from Salesforce and data from other sources.
explanation:
With Wave Analytics in the org and existing Dell Boomi expertise, the split that uses both properly is Wave dataflow for Salesforce-native data and Boomi for the external marketing sources.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Wave dataflow for everything) — dataflow cannot reach the external marketing tools.
Option C (export everything to Excel and import) — manual and not repeatable, so it fails as an ongoing data process.
Option D (Boomi for everything, including Salesforce) — works, but adds an unnecessary ETL hop for data Wave can already read natively.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm

question: Universal Containers manages a catalog of over one million products that it makes available to its customers. The master product catalog is stored and managed in their ERP application with frequent updates made to the product catalog by their sourcing team. The sourcing team may update attributes such as price, general catalog availability, and the product description. When the sourcing team makes an update that change must go into effect during the next business day and there may be thousands of changes made over the course of the day. What integration pattern would you recommend to best manage this scenario?
optionA: Write a custom web service to accept product catalog changes from ERP.
optionB: Use the streaming API to receive product changes in real time from ERP.
optionC: Write an outbound message to send product changes in real time from ERP.
optionD: Build a scheduled ETL job to sync products on a nightly basis from ERP.
explanation:
Thousands of catalog changes a day that only need to take effect by the next business day are a high-volume, non-real-time synchronisation — a scheduled ETL job batching the changes nightly from the ERP.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom web service to accept changes) — code to build and maintain, and it still needs a batching strategy for the volume.
Option B (Streaming API for real-time changes) — real-time delivery the requirement does not ask for, at thousands of events a day.
Option C (outbound message from ERP in real time) — same mismatch, and outbound messaging is a Salesforce-to-external mechanism, not an ERP one.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Universal Containers is integrating their Salesforce platform with their on-premise ERP system. As part of the test class design DML operations are to be performed before making the test callout. What capability does Salesforce provides to facilitate this?
optionA: Perform the DML operation outside the Test.StartTest and Test.StopTest and make the callout outside of the Test.StartTest and Test.StopTest block.
optionB: Perform the DML operation outside the Test.StartTest and Test.StopTest and make the callout with the Test.StartTest and Test.StopTest block.
optionC: Perform the DML operation inside the Test.StartTest and Test.Stop Test and make the callout outside the Test.StartTest and Test.Stop Test block.
optionD: Perform the DML operation within the Test.StartTest and Test.Stop Test and make the callout within Test.StartTest and Test.StopTest block.
explanation:
Perform the DML outside Test.startTest()/Test.stopTest(), then issue the mocked callout inside the block. That ordering separates the uncommitted DML from the callout, and it resets governor limits for the code being measured.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (DML outside, callout also outside) — the callout gains no fresh limits and sits outside the measured block, so the structure the question asks about is not established.
Option C (DML inside, callout outside) — inverts it: the DML is still uncommitted when the callout runs, which is the error this arrangement exists to avoid.
Option D (both inside the block) — DML and callout in the same context raise "You have uncommitted work pending".
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing_dml.htm

question: A company needs to be able to send data from Salesforce to a home grown system behind a corporate firewall. The data needs to be pushed only one way and doesn't need to be sent in real time. The average volume is 2 million records per day. What should an integration architect consider when choosing the right option in building the integration between the external system and Salesforce?
optionA: Due to high volume of records, a third party integration tool is required to stage records off platform.
optionB: Due to high volume of records, number of concurrent requests can hit the limit for the REST API call to external system.
optionC: Due to high volume of records, Salesforce will need to make a REST API call to external system.
optionD: Due to high volume of records, the external system will need to use a Bulk API REST endpoint to connect to Salesforce.
explanation:
The destination sits behind a corporate firewall, so Salesforce cannot open a connection into it. The external system has to initiate the connection outbound from its own network and pull, which is why D is the only option that gets the direction right.
At roughly 2 million records a day, Bulk API 2.0 is the documented fit: Salesforce describes it as REST-based, optimised for large data sets and asynchronous — "you submit a request and come back for the results later" — and puts the threshold far below this volume, at "more than 2,000 records". For an outbound feed the mechanism is a Bulk API 2.0 query job.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a third-party tool is required to stage records off platform) — staging may be convenient for throttling or retries, but the option claims it is required, and it is not: Bulk API 2.0 is a plain REST interface the home-grown system can call itself.
Option B (concurrent request limits on REST calls to the external system) — has Salesforce calling outward, the one thing the firewall prevents.
Option C (Salesforce will need to make a REST API call to the external system) — the same wrong direction, stated outright.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/queries.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#batch-data-synchronization

corrected.note: Q84 A->D. Target sits behind a firewall, so the external system must initiate; Bulk API fits 2M/day one-way.

question: The URL for an external service has been changed without prior notice. The service provides up to date money exchange rates that is accessed several times from Salesforce and is a business critical function for end users. Which two solutions should an Integration Architect recommend be implemented to minimize potential downtime for users in this situation? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Named Credentials
optionB: Remote Site Settings
optionC: Content Security Policies
optionD: Enterprise ESB
explanation:
What shortens the outage is keeping the endpoint somewhere other than compiled code. A Named Credential holds the URL and its authentication as configuration, so a changed endpoint is a field edit that takes effect immediately with no deployment (A). An ESB goes further: Salesforce calls the bus, the new provider URL is repointed in middleware, and every other consumer of that feed is shielded too (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Remote Site Settings) — only an allow-list a callout must satisfy. Updating it does not remove the hardcoded endpoint from Apex, so a deployment is still needed and the downtime stands. A callout through a Named Credential does not consult it at all.
Option C (Content Security Policies) — governs browser-side requests from Lightning components, not Apex callouts.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_trusted_urls_manage.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Q83 A,B -> A,D. Remote Site Settings is a prerequisite for raw callouts, not a way to absorb an endpoint change; Named Credentials and an ESB both externalise the URL from code, which is what shortens the outage.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) use Salesforce to track leads, opportunities, and to capture order details. However, Salesforce isn't the system that holds or processes orders. After the order details are captured in Salesforce, an order must be created in the remote system, which manages the orders lifecylce. The Integration Architect for the project is recommending a remote system that will subscribe to the platform event defined in Salesforce. Which integration pattern should be used for this business use case?
optionA: Batch Data Synchronization
optionB: Request and Reply
optionC: Remote Call In
optionD: Fire and Forget
explanation:
Salesforce captures the order and a remote system subscribes to a Platform Event to create it downstream. Salesforce publishes and moves on with no reply expected, which is Fire and Forget.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Batch Data Synchronization) — scheduled bulk movement, not an event published as the order is captured.
Option B (Request and Reply) — expects a synchronous response, but nothing here waits for one.
Option C (Remote Call In) — describes an external system calling into Salesforce, the opposite direction.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--fire-and-forget
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_subscribe.htm

question: Universal containers decided to use Salesforce sales cloud for their sales processes. Won Opportunities must be sent to external ERP system for order fulfillment. All the line items must also be sent along with Opportunities. The ERP system supports only SOAP- based messages for receiving orders. What limitation of outbound messages might present a problem in this scenario?
optionA: Outbound messaging cannot be made secure
optionB: Outbound messaging does not support multiple objects
optionC: Outbound messaging does not support SOAP
optionD: Outbound messaging does not offer any reliability.
explanation:
Outbound Messaging is built on a single object's WSDL, so it cannot natively send a parent plus its full collection of child line items in one message — which is exactly what "all the line items must also be sent" requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (cannot be made secure) — false; outbound messages are sent over SSL to an HTTPS endpoint.
Option C (does not support SOAP) — false, and backwards: SOAP is the only thing outbound messaging speaks, which is why it suits this ERP.
Option D (offers no reliability) — false; it retries for up to 24 hours until the endpoint acknowledges.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal containers would like to restrict access to Salesforce to only clients on their network. Which two mechanisms should an Integration Architect utilize to prevent unauthorized clients? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Configure Login IP Ranges on any profiles used by Integration
optionB: Use a login flow to validate the IP and request a 2nd factor if incorrect
optionC: Enable the "Lock sessions to the IP address from which they originated" setting.
optionD: Use a trigger to change the user's profile if their IP is not trusted.
explanation:
Login IP Ranges on the profiles used by integrations block logins originating outside the corporate range (A), and a Login Flow can inspect the originating IP and step up to a second factor when it does not match (B).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (lock sessions to the originating IP) — protects a session after login by preventing hijacking; it does not stop an unauthorised client authenticating in the first place.
Option D (trigger to change the user's profile when the IP is untrusted) — reacts after the login has already succeeded, and triggers do not fire on login at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.login_ip_ranges.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An insurance company decides to build an online portal using the Salesforce platform for receiving quote requests from customers. The company has a legacy quoting system that will generate quotes while the rest of the sales process is managed by Salesforce Sales Cloud. The legacy system has an API for creating quotes. What Implementation method should be used so that customers can request quotes online and receive them in real time?
optionA: Outbound message to send quote requests from Salesforce to the legacy system.
optionB: Middleware tool to pull quote requests from SF and push to the legacy system.
optionC: Trigger with an @Future method to send quote requests to the legacy system.
optionD: Apex callout to send quote requests from Salesforce to the legacy System.
explanation:
Customers submitting quote requests from a portal need the generated quote back while they wait, so the call has to be synchronous — an Apex callout to the legacy system's API.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (outbound message) — fire-and-forget SOAP with no reply to return to the customer.
Option B (middleware pulling requests from Salesforce) — a poll adds latency by design and breaks the real-time experience.
Option C (trigger with an @future method) — asynchronous, so the customer's page has nothing to display when it returns.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

question: An Integration Architect has designed a mobile application for Salesforce users to get data while on the road using a custom UI. The application is secured with OAuth and is currently functioning well. There is a new requirement where the mobile application needs to obtain the GPS coordinates and store it on a custom geolocation field. The geolocation field is secured with Field Level Security, so users can view the value without changing it. What should be done to meet the requirement?
optionA: The mobile device makes a REST API inbound call.
optionB: The mobile device makes a REST Apex inbound call.
optionC: The mobile device makes a SOAP API inbound call.
optionD: The mobile device receives a REST Apex callout call.
explanation:
The mobile user cannot write the geolocation field, because field-level security marks it read-only for them. An Apex REST inbound service is the only option that can perform the write, because Apex is where you can explicitly opt a database operation out of the running user's field permissions.
That is an explicit opt-in, not automatic: custom Apex REST methods run in user mode by default, enforcing object permissions, field-level security and sharing. The Apex must deliberately run the operation in system mode, and be declared without sharing if record-level access also needs bypassing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (REST API inbound call) — runs as that user and enforces their field permissions, so the write is rejected.
Option C (SOAP API inbound call) — same enforcement, same rejection.
Option D (the device receives a REST Apex callout) — direction backwards: that is Salesforce calling out, not the device writing data in.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_rest_exposing_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_enforce_usermode.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands at B, but the stated mechanism was wrong. The explanation claimed an Apex REST service "runs in system context" and therefore writes the field automatically; Salesforce documents that custom Apex REST methods run in USER mode by default and enforce field-level security. Apex is still the right answer because it is the only option that can explicitly opt into system mode (WITH SYSTEM_MODE, system-mode DML). Also split option C, which had two distinct options merged into one string, leaving D empty.

question: What are three capabilities of Salesforce outbound messaging? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Build integration components without the Use of APEX.
optionB: Provide a session ID as part of the outbound message.
optionC: Define a WSDL based upon 2 objects related via Master-Detaikls relationship.
optionD: Repeatedly send a SOAP notification for up to 24 hours until an acknowledgement is received.
optionE: Define a custom WSDL based upon an Apex Interface class definition.
explanation:
Outbound messaging is configured entirely in Setup and needs no Apex (A), and it retries the SOAP notification for up to 24 hours until the endpoint acknowledges, after which the message is dropped (D).
Option B is the historically correct third answer and what the exam expects, but it no longer describes the platform: Salesforce removed the session ID from outbound messages in February 2026, so the checkbox is gone, IncludeSessionId is always FALSE and no sessionID element is sent. A receiver must now authenticate with OAuth 2.0. Learn B as keyed; do not design against it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (WSDL across two objects in a master-detail relationship) — the WSDL is generated from a single object, which is the same limitation that makes outbound messaging a poor fit for sending line items.
Option E (custom WSDL from an Apex interface) — outbound messaging generates its WSDL from an object definition; Apex plays no part in it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=005232763&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: DEFECTIVE ITEM, key left at A,B,D. Option B — "provide a session ID as part of the outbound message" — was retired by Salesforce in February 2026, so only A and D are still true capabilities. The stem asks for three, and no fourth true option exists, so the item cannot be repaired by changing the key without breaking the choose-three structure. Key kept to match the exam; explanation now marks B as retired and points to OAuth 2.0.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a leading provider of management training globally. UC requested students course registration data generated from the Salesforce student community to be synced with the learning management system (LMS). Any update to the course registration data needs to be reflected in the LMS. Which integration mechanism should be used to meet the requirement?
optionA: Change Data Capture (CDC)
optionB: Outbound Message
optionC: Platform Event
optionD: Streaming API
explanation:
Keeping the LMS continuously in step with course-registration records is a data-replication requirement, which is what Change Data Capture is built for: create, update, delete and undelete events carrying the changed field values, retained for 72 hours so a subscriber that drops offline resumes from its ReplayId without losing updates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Outbound Message) — targets one fixed SOAP endpoint rather than a subscribing client, and sends a single object without a replay window.
Option C (Platform Event) — you would have to define the event and publish it from automation on every change, hand-building what CDC emits automatically.
Option D (Streaming API) — PushTopic-style notifications are aimed at refreshing a user interface, not at reliably synchronising an external datastore.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_subscribe_delivery.htm

corrected.note: Q93 D->A. Keeping an external system in sync with record changes is CDC's purpose; PushTopic is for UI.

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to connect their on-premise ERP system to view Order data in Salesforce. UC is considering a solution to integrate the on-premise system using Salesforce Connect via OData. Which three considerations should an Architect keep in mind when recommending use of Salesforce Connect?
optionA: Customer wants the ability to query external data using Global Search and reports.
optionB: Customer has a large amount of data that they do not want to load into Salesforce.
optionC: Customer wants to create a master-detail relationship between Opportunity and the external object.
optionD: Customer needs to query small amounts of data at any time and display using a related list.
optionE: Customer does not want real-time access to the ERP data and is willing to wait for hourly refreshes.
explanation:
Salesforce Connect over OData fits when users need to query external data through global search and reports (A), when the data set is large and should not be copied in (B), and when small amounts are fetched on demand for a related list (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (master-detail relationship to the external object) — external objects do not support master-detail; the available relationships are lookup, external lookup and indirect lookup.
Option E (hourly refreshes are acceptable) — describes a replication requirement. If you are content with stale data on a schedule, ETL is the cheaper answer and Salesforce Connect's real-time virtualisation is not what you need.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.external_object_relationships.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A large consumer goods manufacturer operating in multiple countries is planning to implement Salesforce for their Sales and Support operations globally. They have the following security requirements: 1. Internal users from each country have to be authenticated with their local active directory. 2. Customers can create their own login or use Google login. 3. Partners have to be authenticated through a central system which is to be determined. 4. Internal users will have access to the central ERP with their credentials maintained in the ERP. 5. Additional internal systems will be integrated with Salesforce for Sales and Support business processes. Which three requirements should the integration architect evaluate while designing the integration needs of this project? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Evaluate Salesforce native authentication mechanism for all users including customers and partners.
optionB: Evaluate Salesforce solution for customers and for partners, using third party solution for internal users.
optionC: Consider Third party Single Sign On solution supporting all user authentication including customer and partner.
optionD: Assess security requirements for internal systems and decide Integration methods that support the requirements.
optionE: Evaluate the build of a custom authentication mechanism for users in each country and support for customers and partners.
explanation:
Requirement 1 puts internal authentication in each country's local Active Directory. What genuinely needs weighing is a split model — Salesforce handling customers and partners while a third-party IdP handles internal users (B) — against a single third-party SSO covering every population (C), plus the security posture of each internal system and the integration method that satisfies it (D), which is what requirements 4 and 5 demand.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Salesforce-native authentication for all users) — cannot satisfy requirement 1, since local Active Directory authentication needs federation to an external IdP.
Option E (build a custom authentication mechanism per country) — an anti-pattern an architect should reject rather than evaluate, and it multiplies the attack surface by the number of countries.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_jit_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.sso_provider_openid_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Q95 A,D,E->B,C,D. Requirement 1 forces an external IdP, so "Salesforce native for all" fails; custom auth is an anti-pattern.

question: Which two automated methods should an architect use to solve an issue with duplicate contacts? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Enable duplicate management in the org to prevent duplicates.
optionB: Leverage an AppExchange data management toolto de-duplicate contacts.
optionC: Assign new contacts to queues to be reviewed by a data quality team.
optionD: Write a Batch Apex class to manage the deduplication
explanation:
Duplicate Management — matching rules plus duplicate rules — stops duplicates at the point of entry declaratively (A), and a proven AppExchange data-management tool handles the bulk merge of those already in the org (B).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (assign new contacts to a review queue) — explicitly manual, and the question asks for automated methods.
Option D (Batch Apex deduplication class) — automated, but it means building and maintaining custom merge logic when a packaged solution already covers it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sales.managing_duplicates_overview.htm&type=5

corrected.note: Q96 A,D->A,B. Declarative/packaged over custom Apex; C is manual.

question: Universal Containers has Logistics Engineers that observe a near real-time dashboard in Salesforce of shipping containers that are in transit. Without leaving the dashboard, an Engineer can select a container to request an updated status on that container. These requests are handled by a proprietary shipping system that queues the requests to send to each container. Containers are connected devices and check in with the shipping system every 30 seconds to receive any status requests. What integration pattern or combination of patterns would be needed to connect Salesforce and the shipping system?
optionA: UI Update Based on Data Changes and Batch Data Synchronization
optionB: Remote Call-In, with UI Update Based on Data Changes
optionC: Remote Process Invocation-Fire and Forget, with UI Update Based on Data Changes
optionD: Remote Process Invocation-Request and Reply
explanation:
The engineer triggers an on-demand request, but the proprietary system queues it for devices that only check in every 30 seconds, so nothing can be answered synchronously. Send the request with Remote Process Invocation – Fire and Forget, then refresh the dashboard with UI Update Based on Data Changes once the status arrives.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (UI Update plus Batch Data Synchronization) — the UI half is right, but a scheduled batch does not carry the engineer's on-demand request outward.
Option B (Remote Call-In plus UI Update) — Remote Call-In is inbound, so it does not send the request to the shipping system.
Option D (Request and Reply) — blocks waiting for a response the shipping system cannot give until the container next checks in.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--fire-and-forget

question: Universal Containers is using Sales Could with Order Capture. It has been integrated with an SAP system for Order fulfillment. The SAP system sends the Order status updates to Salesforce on a nightly basis. The SAP system tracks Order status more granularly than required by Salesforce. Which two options should an Architect recommend to address different statuses in Salesforce and SAP?
optionA: ETL Change Data Capture interface to send only required status updates to Salesforce.
optionB: Create a batch Apex to run on a daily basis, which converts order status to pre-defined order status.
optionC: Update the SAP Order fulfillment process to match Salesforce Order Statuses against the SAP order status.
optionD: ETL change Data capture interface transforms the SAP order statuses to Salesforce order status.
explanation:
Salesforce tracks order status more coarsely than SAP, so the integration must map SAP's granular values before loading. An ETL or Change Data Capture interface can both filter to the statuses Salesforce needs (A) and perform the transformation between the two sets (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (daily Batch Apex converting statuses) — puts mapping logic on-platform and leaves unmapped values sitting in Salesforce until the job next runs.
Option C (change SAP to match Salesforce statuses) — asks the system of record to lose granularity it needs for fulfilment, to suit a downstream consumer.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_intro.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has an affiliate company that would like immediate notifications of changes to opportunities in the NTO Salesforce instance. The affiliate company has a CometD client available. Which solution is recommended in order to meet the requirement?
optionA: A Implement a polling mechanism in the client that calls the SOAP API getupdated method to get the ID values of each updated record.
optionB: Configure External Services to call the subscriber in Apex in the Onchange Trigger event as part of the flow.
optionC: Create a connected app in the affiliate org and select the "Accept CometD API Requests".
optionD: Create a PushTopic update event on the Opportunity Object to allow the subscriber to react to the streaming API.
explanation:
The affiliate already runs a CometD client and wants immediate notice of Opportunity changes, which is what a PushTopic on the Streaming API provides: the subscriber receives change events as they happen.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (poll the SOAP getUpdated method) — polling is not immediate, and it wastes API calls on intervals with no changes.
Option B (External Services calling the subscriber from a trigger) — External Services invokes an external REST action from Flow; it is not a subscription mechanism, and it would not deliver to a CometD client.
Option C ("Accept CometD API Requests" on a connected app in the affiliate org) — no such setting exists, and the connected app would belong to the NTO org rather than the affiliate's.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_streaming.meta/api_streaming/pushtopic_events_intro.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) leverages Sales Cloud for tracking and managing leads, accounts, contacts, and opportunities. Orders and order fulfillment is taken care of by an Order Management System (OMS) in the back-office. When an opportunity has changed it's status to "Closed/Won" and there are products attached, the details should be passed to the OMS for fulfillment operations. The callout from Salesforce to the OMS should be synchronous. What should an Integration Architect do to satisfy these requirements?
optionA: Write a trigger that invokes an Apex proxy class to make a REST callout to the Order Management System.
optionB: Develop a batch Apex job that aggregates Closed Opportunities and makes a REST callout to the Order Management System hourly.
optionC: Build a Lightning Component that makes a synchronous Apex REST callout to the Order Management System when a button is clicked.
optionD: Use Process Builder to call an Apex proxy class to make a REST callout to the Order Management System.
explanation:
Of the options offered, Process Builder calling an Apex proxy class is the one that fires automatically when the Opportunity reaches Closed/Won, which is what the scenario describes.
Two caveats matter more than the letter. First, the stem's demand for a synchronous callout cannot actually be met by any automatic option here: Salesforce documents that you cannot make a callout with pending operations in the same transaction, and DML is such an operation, so an Apex proxy invoked after save must be @future(callout=true) — which makes it asynchronous. Treat D as the automation answer, not the synchronous one. Second, Process Builder reached end of support on 31 December 2025; existing processes still run, but a design built today would use Flow.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (trigger invoking an Apex proxy) — a trigger cannot call out directly, so it necessarily defers to @future or Queueable, which is the same asynchrony the item objects to.
Option B (hourly batch of closed Opportunities) — hourly by definition, so it is neither immediate nor synchronous.
Option C (Lightning Component with a synchronous callout on a button click) — genuinely synchronous, but it only runs when a user clicks, so it does not respond to a status change.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_timeouts.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

corrected.note: Key D stands, but the item is defective and the explanation now says so instead of asserting Process Builder is 'the supported path' for a synchronous callout. Two problems. The pending-DML rule means a callout from Process Builder-invoked Apex requires @future(callout=true), so it is asynchronous — which contradicts the stem's synchronous requirement and undercuts the explanation's own reason for rejecting option A. No option satisfies both 'automatic on status change' and 'synchronous', so the stem is internally inconsistent. Separately, Process Builder hit end of support on 31 Dec 2025; per the established fact that this is retirement of support rather than removal of capability, the key remains correct, and Flow is the current equivalent. Flagged for the user: the clean repair is to drop 'synchronous' from the stem, or reword option D to name Flow.

question: Universal Containers is a global financial company that sells financial products and services. There is a daily scheduled Batch Apex job that generates invoice from a given set of orders. UC requested building a resilient integration for this batch apex job in case the invoice generation fails. What should an integration architect recommend to fulfill the requirement?
optionA: Build Batch Retry & Error Handling in the middleware.
optionB: Build Batch Retry & Error Handling using BatchApexErrorEvent.
optionC: Build Batch Retry & Error Handling in the Batch Apex Job itself.
optionD: Batch Retry & Error Handling report to monitor the error handling.
explanation:
BatchApexErrorEvent is the platform event raised on an unhandled exception in a batch job. Subscribing to it captures the failure context and lets retry or error handling run automatically, which is what makes the scheduled job resilient.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (retry and error handling in middleware) — middleware cannot see a failure that happens inside a Salesforce batch job.
Option C (retry inside the Batch Apex job itself) — the job cannot catch the failure that aborted it, which is the case that matters.
Option D (a report to monitor error handling) — surfaces failures after the fact for a human to read; it recovers nothing.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/sforce_api_objects_batchapexerrorevent.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2019/01/building-a-batch-retry-framework-with-batchapexerrorevent

question: Universal Containers has chosen Salesforce Wave as their Analytics Platform. There is a requirement to join data from multiple systems(including Salesforce) to be displayed in a single Wave Lens. What should the Architect recommend?
optionA: Use data flow to load Salesforce data,and lightning connect to access the other data sets in real time.
optionB: Use an ETL tool to join multiple sources and load them into a single data set.
optionC: Use an ETL tool to load the data into Salesforce, upserts to ensure that the data in properly joined.
optionD: Use Data flow to load Salesforce data, and an ETL tool to load other data sets.
