explanation:
Joining several sources, Salesforce included, into one lens means combining them before they reach Analytics — an ETL tool that joins the sources and loads a single prepared dataset.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (dataflow plus Lightning Connect for real-time access) — external objects are not a source Analytics can join into a dataset, and virtualised access does not survive into a lens.
Option C (ETL everything into Salesforce and upsert to join) — bloats the org with data it has no operational use for, purely to stage a join.
Option D (dataflow for Salesforce, ETL for the rest) — loads the sources separately, leaving two datasets when the requirement is one joined lens.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm

question: Universal Containers requires Salesforce to send expense data to an accounting system. Each user has their own username/password credential to access the account system via integration. What is a recommended option for an integration approach from a security perspective?
optionA: Fire outbound messages to a middleware that stores the credentials instead of an Apex callout.
optionB: Use hierarchical custom settings to store the username/password allowing the Apex callout to read it.
optionC: Set up a Per-User Named Credential and have the users each set up their username/password.
optionD: Set up a Named-Principal Named Credential and have the administrator set up the username/password.
explanation:
Each user holds their own credentials for the accounting system, so a Per-User Named Credential is the fit: every user supplies and stores their own username and password in the platform's protected store, and the callout authenticates as that user.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (outbound messages to middleware holding the credentials) — collapses per-user identity into whatever the middleware stores, losing the per-user authentication the stem describes.
Option B (hierarchical custom settings holding the password) — leaves credentials readable to anyone who can see the record or the metadata.
Option D (Named-Principal Named Credential) — secure, but shares one identity across all users, which contradicts "each user has their own credential".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.platform_connect_identity_type.htm&type=5

question: Universal Containers would like to display data from an external system inside of Salesforce, and has chosen not to enable Lightning Experience. They do not need the data for any other purposes within Salesforce. Which approach should an Integration Architect recommend that matches the Salesforce UI? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: A middleware orchestration to continuously persist data from other systems into Salesforce.
optionB: A custom visualforce page with a controller thats calls-out to the other systems.
optionC: An iFrame embedding a custom .Net application that displays data from the other systems.
optionD: A custom Visualforce page with client- side calls out to the other systems.
explanation:
The stem sets two tests: the data must not persist in Salesforce, and the result must match the Salesforce UI. A Visualforce page inherits the platform styling, so it passes both whether the external call is made server-side from its controller (B) or client-side from JavaScript on the page (D) — the two genuinely different implementations offered. Lightning Experience being switched off is what makes Visualforce rather than a Lightning component the vehicle.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (middleware continuously persisting the data) — fails the first test: the company has said it needs the data for nothing else in Salesforce.
Option C (iframe embedding a custom .NET application) — renders that application's own interface inside Salesforce, which is the opposite of matching the Salesforce UI however convenient it is to build.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pages.meta/pages/pages_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_connect.meta/platform_connect/canvas_framework_intro.htm

corrected.note: Q102 B,C -> B,D. The stem asks for approaches that match the Salesforce UI; an iframe hosting a .NET application is precisely what does not.

question: Universal Containers sells its products online using a system built on Force.com sites. The orders are captures and processed in Salesforce. The company uses an external marketing system and would like to make use of the customer data captured in Salesforce. The marketing system has REST API that can be used to push data into it. Which three options should a Technical Architect consider that do not require building custom web services on the marketing system? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Use a middleware tool to pull customer data from Salesforce and push it to the marketing system on adaily basis.
optionB: Build a custom java application using the Enterprise WSDL to pull data from Salesforce and push it to the marketing system.
optionC: Use outbound messages to send customer data from Salesforce to the marketing system.
optionD: Use Apex callout to send customer data from Salesforce to the marketing system
optionE: Write a custom Apex web service, Which will be called from the marketing system to retrieve customer data.
explanation:
The marketing system already exposes a REST API, so the job is to reach it without building anything new on that side. Middleware can extract and push on a schedule (A), an Apex callout can send the data to the REST API directly (D), and a custom Apex web service lets the marketing system pull the data itself (E) — none of which requires new services on the marketing platform.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (custom Java application over the Enterprise WSDL) — a whole application to build and host, when the REST API can be called directly.
Option C (outbound messages) — sends SOAP, so the marketing system would have to build a SOAP endpoint, which is precisely the constraint the question excludes.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_rest_exposing_data.htm

question: Universal containers is hearing complaints from users that recently released changes, while they meet the functional requirements, are not actually usable and/or do not meet their expectations for user experience. For example, a Visualforce page that takes too long to display the first page of data. Which two types of testing should a technical Architect implement to reduce or eliminate the complaint? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Performance testing
optionB: Regression Testing
optionC: user Acceptance Testing
optionD: Unit Testing
explanation:
Changes that are functionally correct but slow or disappointing point at two gaps: Performance testing catches the slow page load named in the stem (A), and User Acceptance Testing confirms the result matches what users actually expected (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Regression Testing) — verifies that existing behaviour still works; these features work, they are just unpleasant to use.
Option D (Unit Testing) — checks components in isolation against expected outputs, which says nothing about page load time or user expectations.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/data-cloud-dev/guide/dc-app-lifecycle.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2025/02/load-test-on-the-salesforce-platform-using-scalability-tools

question: A company that is a leading provider of courses and training delivers courses using third party trainers. The trainer for the company has to be verified from 10 different training accreditation verification agencies before providing training for the company. Each training accreditation agency has its own response time, which could take days to confirm a trainer. The company decided to automate the trainer accreditation verification process by integrating to the agencies web services. What is the recommended approach to automate this process?
optionA: Create a trigger on the trainer record to make a Callout to each verification agencies, write business logic to consolidate the verification then update the trainer status to verified".
optionB: Make an apex callout using @future annotation to make the call out to all differentagencies. The response should update the trainer status to "verified".
optionC: Use salesforce external service to make the call out, Salesforce external service should check the verification agencies until the result is verified, then update the trainer status to "verified".
optionD: Use middleware to handle the call out to the 10 different verification services, the middleware will handle the business logic of consolidating the verification result from t 10 services, then make a call-in to sa lesforce and update the verification status to "verified".
explanation:
Verification depends on ten agencies with independent, possibly multi-day response times, so the waiting and consolidation belong in middleware: it calls all ten, applies the logic to consolidate results, then calls back into Salesforce to set the trainer to verified.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (trigger calling out to each agency) — a trigger cannot call out directly, and nothing in a transaction can wait days for ten replies.
Option B (@future callouts to all agencies) — asynchronous but still bounded by transaction limits, with no way to hold state across days or consolidate ten separate responses.
Option C (External Services polling until verified) — External Services drives declarative synchronous actions from Flow; it has no mechanism for a multi-day waiting state.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: In order to avoid slowing down inbound call center sales agents, Universal Containers wants to de-duplicate Lead records against their 3rd-party MDM system after that the agent has served the record in Salesforce. What integration strategy should an Architect recommend?
optionA: Use Out-of-the-Box Lead De-duplication Rules to checkagainst MDM.
optionB: Batch APEX process to de-duplicate all records first in Salesforce then against MDM, deleting the newest MDM record.
optionC: Sync the MDM system to a custom object in Salesforce and execute a Lookup validation rule against the object.
optionD: Outbound message to MDM with a callback to Salesforce to mark duplicate Leads.
explanation:
De-duplicating against the external MDM only after the agent has finished with the lead is what keeps the agent fast, so the check has to be asynchronous: an outbound message to the MDM with a callback that marks duplicate Leads in Salesforce.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (out-of-the-box Lead duplicate rules) — native duplicate management compares records inside Salesforce and cannot reach the MDM.
Option B (Batch Apex de-duplicating then deleting the newest MDM record) — runs across all records rather than the one just served, and deleting in the MDM inverts which system is master.
Option C (sync the MDM to a custom object with a lookup validation rule) — copies the entire MDM into Salesforce, and a validation rule would block the agent at save time, which is the slowdown being avoided.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sales.managing_duplicates_overview.htm&type=5

question: Universal Containers has a homegrown application that polls Salesforce using SOAP API every 2 minutes to obtain newly created case information. This causes both performance issues and API usage limits to be exceeded. What should an Architect recommend to improve performance and optimum use the API limits?
optionA: Use REST API to identify new case records in Salesforce every 15 minutes.
optionB: Use an Apex callout to identify new case records and send them to the client.
optionC: Use Generic Streaming to send push notifications of case creation events to the client.
optionD: Use Streaming API to publish new case records to a push topic and subscribe to it.
explanation:
Polling with SOAP every two minutes spends API calls whether or not anything changed. Publishing new Cases to a PushTopic and letting the client subscribe over the Streaming API delivers them as events, with no per-poll cost.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (REST polling every 15 minutes) — still polling; it trades freshness for a smaller bill without fixing the mechanism.
Option B (Apex callout to send new cases to the client) — inverts the design into Salesforce-initiated callouts, one per case, with its own limits.
Option C (Generic Streaming) — a channel for arbitrary messages you publish yourself; it is not raised by record creation, so something else would have to detect the new Case.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_streaming.meta/api_streaming/pushtopic_events_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has third-party MDM database which is responsible for maintaining the data for Customer and Contacts information for its organization. UC wants to keep this information up-to-date in Salesforce so that the information is as current as possible. UC wants to provide bi-directional synchronization of the data between the MDM and Salesforce. What is the recommended approach to solving this problem?
optionA: Modify the MDM database application to send and receive updates to and from Salesforce via REST or SOAP as they occur.
optionB: Create a Batch process that runs every 5 minutes to pull the changes from MDM and any updates from Salesforce.
optionC: Implement a third-party middleware tool to maintain the synchronization between Salesforce and the MDM database as they occur.
optionD: Create a VisualForce page for Accounts/Contacts that will pull the data from MDM, display it, and send any changes from Salesforce.
explanation:
Bidirectional, as-it-happens synchronisation between an external MDM and Salesforce is what a middleware tool brokers: it watches both sides, applies mapping and conflict rules, and keeps them in step.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (modify the MDM application to send and receive directly) — point-to-point and brittle, putting Salesforce-specific logic inside the MDM.
Option B (batch every 5 minutes pulling both directions) — polling, so it is never truly as changes occur, and two-way polling invites conflicts.
Option D (Visualforce page pulling and pushing) — only synchronises records while someone is looking at them.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

question: Universal Containers is planning a data migration into Salesforce and must decide whether to use the Bulk API or the SOAP API. Which three statements are true about the Bulk API and REST API? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: DML limits on Bulk are not governed on Salesforce servers.
optionB: The Bulk API allows multiple attachments to be leaded from within a single ZIP file.
optionC: The SOAP API avoids record locking contention on parent objects of Master-Details relationship.
optionD: The SOAP API provides jpb monitoring on the Salesforce setup menu.
optionE: The Bulk API may cause record locking contension on parent objects od Master-Details relationship.
explanation:
Three statements hold. The Bulk API accepts multiple binary attachments in a single ZIP with a request.txt manifest (B). Bulk processes large batches in parallel, which can produce record-locking contention on the parent of a master-detail relationship when children of the same parent land in different batches (E), while the SOAP API's smaller synchronous transactions avoid that contention (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (DML limits on Bulk are not governed on Salesforce servers) — the weakest statement in the set: Bulk operations are still governed, just under asynchronous limits rather than synchronous ones.
Option D (SOAP provides job monitoring in the Setup menu) — backwards: the Bulk Data Load Jobs monitor is a Bulk API feature.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/binary_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2014/08/managing-task-locks-data-loads

corrected.note: Q112 A,C,E->B,C,E. Bulk ZIP attachment loading is documented; option A's wording is not defensible.

question: Northern Trail Outfitters' ERP is integrated with Salesforce and syncs several million contacts per day. To prevent specific data from syncing, the integration uses a SOQL query filtered by sharing hierarchy. Which two things should an architect do to improve the performance of the integration? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Include non-selective criteria in query filters.
optionB: Remove the query filters.
optionC: Include selective criteria in query filters.
optionD: Remove the sharing restrictions.
explanation:
A SOQL-driven integration filtered by the sharing hierarchy over millions of contacts improves in two ways: make the query selective, so indexed criteria let the optimizer avoid a full scan (C), and remove the sharing restrictions that force it to evaluate sharing row by row (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (include non-selective criteria) — the opposite of the fix: non-selective filters are what push the optimizer into a full scan.
Option B (remove the query filters) — returns even more rows, making the problem worse rather than better.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/engineering/2013/07/maximizing-the-performance-of-force-com-soql-reports-and-list-views
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_infrastructure_indexes.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has hired an Integration Architect to design the integrations between existing systems and a new instance of Salesforce. NTO has the following requirements: 1. Initial load of 2M Accounts,5.5M Contacts, 4.3M Opportunities, and 45k Products into the new org. 2. Notification of new and updated Accounts and Contacts needs to be sent to 3 external systems. 3. Expose custom business logic to 5 external applications in a highly secure manner. 4. Schedule nightly automated dataflows, recipes and data syncs. Which set of APIs are recommended in order to meet the requirements?
optionA: Bulk API, Streaming API, Apex REST API, Analytics REST API
optionB: Bulk API, Streaming API, Apex SOAP API, Analytics REST API
optionC: Bulk API, Chatter REST API, Apex SOAP API, Tooling API
optionD: Bulk API, Chatter REST API, Apex REST API, Analytics REST API
explanation:
The four requirements map cleanly: Bulk API for the multi-million-record initial load, Streaming API to notify three external systems of new and updated Accounts and Contacts, Apex REST API to expose custom business logic securely to five applications, and Analytics REST API for the nightly dataflows, recipes and syncs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Apex SOAP API instead of Apex REST) — workable but heavier for exposing logic to five modern applications, and REST is the recommended surface.
Option C (Chatter REST and Tooling API) — Chatter REST serves feeds and Tooling serves metadata; neither notifies external systems nor runs analytics dataflows.
Option D (Chatter REST instead of Streaming) — Chatter REST cannot deliver record-change notifications to three subscribers.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_rest_exposing_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm

question: Universal Containers requires Salesforce to send order data to an ERP system that requires a system-defined username/password for authentication. Which two integration options are recommended from a security perspective?
optionA: Store the username/hashed password in a private Static Resource, allowing the Apex callout to read it.
optionB: Use custom settings to store the username and password allowing the Apex callout to read it.
optionC: Fire outbound messages to a middleware that stores the credentials instead of an Apex callout.
optionD: Set up a Named Credential with a Named Principal Identity Type allowing the Apex callout to use it.
explanation:
Both recommended options keep the ERP credential out of anything a Salesforce user or developer can read. A Named Credential with a Named Principal identity type holds the system username and password in the platform's protected store and injects them at runtime, so the secret never appears in Apex (D). Delegating the call to middleware that holds the credential achieves the same separation, leaving Salesforce with no copy at all (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (username and hashed password in a private static resource) — static resources are metadata, readable by anyone who can retrieve them, and a hash cannot be replayed as a password anyway.
Option B (custom settings holding the username and password) — leaves the secret readable to anyone with access to the record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.secure_coding_guide.meta/secure_coding_guide/secure_coding_storing_sensitive_data.htm

question: Which two options should be considered to permit automatic retry of failed updates when loading data into Salesforce? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Bulk API with serial option.
optionB: Standard API with serial option.
optionC: Standard API with parallel option.
optionD: Bulk API with parallel option.
explanation:
Automatic retry of failed records on load is a Bulk API behaviour, and it applies in both processing modes — serial (A) and parallel (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (standard API with serial option) — the SOAP API has no equivalent automatic retry of failed batches; failures come back for the client to handle.
Option C (standard API with parallel option) — same gap, and "parallel" is not a mode the standard API offers in this sense.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Universal Containers is hearing complaints from users that recently released changes are breaking existing functionality. What type of testing program should a Technical Architect implement to reduce or eliminate this complaint?
optionA: User Acceptance Testing
optionB: Unit Testing
optionC: Regression Testing
optionD: Performance Testing
explanation:
Users reporting that new releases break what previously worked is the definition of a regression, and Regression Testing is the programme that re-verifies existing behaviour after every change.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (User Acceptance Testing) — confirms new features meet requirements, rather than systematically re-checking old ones.
Option B (Unit Testing) — validates components in isolation and routinely passes while cross-component behaviour breaks.
Option D (Performance Testing) — measures speed and scale, not functional correctness.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/data-cloud-dev/guide/dc-app-lifecycle.html

question: An integration architect needs to build a solution that will be using the Streaming API, but the data loss should be minimized, even when the client re-connects every couple of days. Which two types of Streaming API events should be considered? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Change Data Capture Events
optionB: Generic Events
optionC: High Volume Platform Events
optionD: PushTopic Events
explanation:
Surviving a client that reconnects days later needs durable retention and replay. Change Data Capture events (A) and High-Volume Platform Events (C) are both stored for 72 hours and can be replayed from a stored ReplayId.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Generic Events) — retained far more briefly, so a multi-day disconnect loses messages.
Option D (PushTopic Events) — same short retention; PushTopics are built to refresh a live UI, not to survive an outage.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/pub-sub-api/guide/event-message-durability.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_streaming.meta/api_streaming/pushtopic_events_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers acquires several companies and decides to consolidate all customer service systems used by the acquired companies into one Salesforce Service Cloud. They decide to use an ETL to extract service requests from various systems, apply appropriate transformations, and load cases into Salesforce. Different requests captured by different customer service systems could belong to common accounts in Salesforce, so care must be taken to avoid creating duplicate accounts. Which two API options should be considered to load cases into Salesforce that would be safe from record-locking issues? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: SOAP API with a batch size of 200 or less
optionB: Bulk API with serial option and a batch size of 1000 or less
optionC: SOAP API with a batch size of 1000 or less
optionD: Bulk API with parallel option and a batch size of 1000 or less
explanation:
Avoiding lock contention on shared parent Accounts means limiting how many batches touch the same parent at once: the SOAP API with a batch size of 200 or less (A), and the Bulk API in serial mode with batches of 1000 or less (B), which processes one batch at a time.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (SOAP API with a batch size of 1000 or less) — exceeds the SOAP API's 200-record limit, so it is not a valid configuration.
Option D (Bulk API in parallel mode) — maximises the locking risk, which is the failure the question is trying to avoid.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_calls_update.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Universal Containers would like to update their accounting system every time an opportunity is changed to Closed-Won. Their accounting system occasionally is offline for 3-4 hours to support month-end processing, and they would like the integration design to ensure that no transactions are lost during this down time. Which two integration designs should the architect consider? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Utilize workflow outbound messaging, which has a built-in queuing framework.
optionB: Utilize an Apex trigger with an @future class to callout to the accounting system after the month-end processing is complete.
optionC: Utilize the enterprise WSDL to query Salesforce from the Accounting system for opportunities that have changed to Closed-Won.
optionD: Utilize an Enterprise Service Bus to the web service calls between Salesforce and the accounting System.
explanation:
Losing nothing across a 3–4 hour outage needs durable queuing and retry. Workflow outbound messaging retries for up to 24 hours until acknowledged (A), and an ESB can queue the calls and deliver them once the accounting system returns (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (@future callout after month-end processing) — @future has no durable queue and no retry, and nothing in Salesforce knows when month-end processing finished.
Option C (accounting system queries Salesforce over the Enterprise WSDL) — turns the design into polling, and while it would eventually find the records, it inverts the trigger and depends on the accounting system remembering to ask.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--fire-and-forget

question: What are the two considerations of Apex REST services that an integration architect should keep in mind when building custom integrations? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: They cannot utilize publisher actions.
optionB: They require unit and functional testing
optionC: They consume more API limits than SOAP or REST API
optionD: They cannot be built or maintained declaratively
explanation:
Two considerations follow from Apex REST services being code: they require dedicated unit and functional testing before deployment (B), and they cannot be built or maintained declaratively, so every change is a development cycle (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (cannot utilize publisher actions) — not a consideration for designing a custom integration surface.
Option C (consume more API limits than SOAP or REST API) — false; an Apex REST call counts the same as any other API call.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_rest_exposing_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing.htm

question: A company's cloud-based single page application consolidates data local to the application with data from on premise and 3rd party systems. The diagram below typifies the application's combined use of synchronous and asynchronous calls. The company wants to use the average response time of its application's user interface as a basis for certain alerts. For this purpose, the following occurs: 1. Log every call's start and finish date and time to a central analytics data store. 2. Compute response time uniformly as the difference between the start and finish date and time - A to H in the diagram. Which computation represents the end-to-end response time from the user's perspective?
optionA: Sum of A to H
optionB: Sum of A and H
optionC: Sum of A to F
optionD: Sum of A, G, and H
explanation:
Leg A is the UI Component's call to the Middleware, and it does not close until 2.4 returns the consolidated summary — so legs B through F all run inside A and are already counted by it. Leg G is the asynchronous process started at 2.3, which continues after the Middleware has replied and never delays the user. What remains is leg H, the render, so perceived end-to-end time is A + H.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (sum of A to H) — double-counts B through F, which are nested inside A, and adds the async leg the user never waits on.
Option C (sum of A to F) — double-counts the nested legs and stops before the render the user actually sees.
Option D (sum of A, G and H) — folds in the asynchronous process, which by definition finishes after the reply.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

corrected.note: Q122 answer B confirmed against the diagram. The textual rendering added then was replaced on 2026-08-11 by a drawn sequence diagram, which shows the leg nesting the prose could not.

question: Universal Containers has a back-end ordering system that restricts access on a per-user basis. It was determined that a "Named Credential" will be used to allow per-user identity type access for all integration with the system. One of the requirements is to have order information sent to the system when the status changes to "Confirmed". Which two valid integration scenarios can take advantage of such a security setup?
optionA: Order information sent to the system via outbound message with session ID.
optionB: Order information sent via process builder via invokable method/future method callout.
optionC: Order information inserted or updated via Salesforce Connect: OData 2.0.
optionD: Order information sent via a Visualforce page with an Apex callout.
explanation:
A per-user Named Credential only helps where the callout runs as an identifiable user. Process Builder invoking an invocable or @future Apex callout preserves that context, since asynchronous Apex runs as the user who triggered it (B). Salesforce Connect with the OData 2.0 adapter supports a per-user identity type for external object reads and writes, so it qualifies too (C).
Currency note: Process Builder reached end of support on 31 December 2025. Existing processes still run, so B remains correct, but Flow is the mechanism for new work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (outbound message with session ID) — fails on identity: outbound messaging runs as the automated process user, defeating per-user identity. It also rests on a retired capability, since Salesforce removed the session ID from outbound messages in February 2026.
Option D (Visualforce page with an Apex callout) — worth pausing on, because the security setup is not what disqualifies it: such a page genuinely can use a per-user Named Credential. It fails because the requirement is to send on status change, and a Visualforce page waits for someone to open it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Key B,C stands; this is a currency fix rather than a correction. The explanation described Process Builder as the mechanism that 'preserves that context' without noting it reached end of support on 31 Dec 2025, so a reader would take it as current guidance. Added the retirement and named Flow as the replacement, keeping the key because retirement of support is not removal of capability. Also strengthened the rejection of option A, which the old text dismissed only on the automated-process-user grounds: the session ID it depends on was removed from outbound messages in February 2026, so the option describes a capability that no longer exists at all.

question: Universal Containers would like to integrate Salesforce to their Accounting system. Salesforce must notify the accounting system for every new account that has been created. The security team will not allow Salesforce to integrate directly to the accounting system due to potential security issues. Which three stages should the Architect consider to reduce the security concerns for this Integration use case? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Whitelist the Salesforce IP range on the firewall to ensure only Salesforce- originated traffic can penetrate the network.
optionB: Enable platform encryption in the Salesforce org to ensure network communication to the Accounting system is encrypted.
optionC: Enable WS-security for the web services made between Salesforce and the accounting system.
optionD: Utilize an Enterprise Service Bus to ensure Accounting system credentials are not stores within Salesforce.
optionE: Terminate the SSL connection at a reverse proxy in the DMZ which establishes trust in the connection using mutual SSL.
explanation:
Since security forbids Salesforce calling the accounting system directly, the exposure is reduced at the network edge: allow-list the Salesforce IP ranges on the firewall so only that traffic is accepted (A), use an ESB so accounting credentials are never stored in Salesforce (D), and terminate SSL at a DMZ reverse proxy that establishes trust with mutual SSL (E).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (platform encryption in the org) — protects data at rest inside Salesforce and does nothing about the network path or the direct-connection concern.
Option C (WS-Security on the web services) — message-level security is useful, but on its own it still leaves Salesforce connecting straight to the accounting system, which is the objection.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_networkaccess.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_keys_uploading_mutual_auth_cert_api.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers merges with Planetary Shipping. They decide to consolidate their systems and migrate all the customer accounts into one Salesforce org. After some data analysis, they find out that their systems have common accounts that they would like to merge and avoid duplicate accounts in Salesforce. They find out that customer email, available in both the systems, can be used to match common accounts. The customer data can be exported as CSV files from their systems. Which two options should be considered to load accounts into Salesforce and eliminate duplicate accounts? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: ETL tool that is capable of identifying common accounts using email address and performs updates
optionB: Dataloader insert operation and Saleforce's native deduplication after the load
optionC: Dataloader upsert operation with a custom External ID field containing the email address
optionD: ETL tool that is capable of identifying common accounts using a Salesforce ID and performing updates
explanation:
Merging CSV account data from two systems on a shared email key can be done with an ETL tool that matches common accounts by email address and updates them (A), or with Data Loader's upsert against a custom External Id field populated with the email (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Data Loader insert, then native de-duplication) — creates the duplicates first and asks a second process to clean them up, which the requirement is trying to avoid.
Option D (ETL matching on Salesforce Id) — the incoming records have no Salesforce Id yet, so there is nothing to match on.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_calls_upsert.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters needs to secure an integration with an external Microsoft Azure API Gateway. What integration security mechanism should be employed?
optionA: Implement Salesforce Shield with Encryption at Rest and generate a tenant secret.
optionB: Use an API only user profile and implement use an external identity provider with federated API access.
optionC: Configure mutual server authentication with two-way SSL using CA issued certificates.
optionD: Configure a connected app with an authorization endpoint of the API gateway and configure OAuth settings.
explanation:
Securing an integration with an external Azure API Gateway is a transport-trust problem between two systems, which is what mutual two-way SSL with CA-issued certificates solves: each side verifies the other's certificate.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Shield with encryption at rest and a tenant secret) — protects stored data, not the connection to the gateway.
Option B (API-only user profile with a federated external identity provider) — addresses which user may sign in, not how the two endpoints trust each other.
Option D (connected app with the gateway as authorization endpoint) — configures OAuth for user authorisation, which is a different control from gateway-to-gateway transport trust.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_keys_uploading_mutual_auth_cert_api.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) uses Salesforce to track leads, opportunities and order details that convert leads to customers. However, Orders are managed by an external (remote) system. Sales representatives want to view and update real-time order information in Salesforce. NTO wants the data to only persist in the external system. Which type of Integration should an architect recommend to meet this business requirement?
optionA: Data Virtualization
optionB: Data Synchronization
optionC: Process Orchestration
optionD: Batch Processing
explanation:
Sales representatives need to read and write live order data that must never be copied into Salesforce, which is Data Virtualization: Salesforce Connect exposes the remote orders as external objects, queried on demand and written straight back to the source.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Data Synchronization) — works by landing copies in Salesforce, which the requirement forbids.
Option C (Process Orchestration) — coordinates multi-step processes across systems rather than surfacing a remote record for viewing and editing.
Option D (Batch Processing) — also copies data in, and on a schedule, so it is neither local-free nor real time.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect_odata.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Q124 option A read "Data Visualization", which names a different concept entirely. The pattern is Data Virtualization; the answer was always A.

question: Universal Containers has a SOAP-based integration that runs nightly to update the Product(Product2) object in Salesforce with updated product availability for over 500,000 products. The source system is a green-screen ERP that must be taken offline to produce nightly production reports, such as the inventory availability report used for this integration. The integration is performing very slowly and does not complete within the allocated four-hour time slot. What three recommendations might a Technical Architect make to resolve this issue? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Store the Salesforce Product ID in the source system to eliminate the need for External IDs and UPSERT API calls.
optionB: Use the Bulk API UPDATE or UPSERT records more efficiently.
optionC: Use outbound Messaging to notify Salesforce promptly when product availability changes in the source system.
optionD: Pre-process the data to avoid the need for workflow rules or triggers
optionE: Contact Salesforce support to request that they turn off record locking on the Product2 object.
explanation:
Three changes get 500,000 product updates inside the window: store the Salesforce Product Id in the source so the load updates by Id and skips External-Id matching overhead (A), use the Bulk API for efficient UPDATE or UPSERT at that volume (B), and pre-process the data so workflow rules and triggers are not needed during the load (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (outbound messaging when availability changes) — a Salesforce-to-external mechanism, so it cannot push ERP changes inward, and it does not suit a bulk nightly update in any case.
Option E (ask Salesforce Support to turn off record locking on Product2) — not something Salesforce disables on request; locking is how the platform protects data integrity.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_calls_upsert.htm

question: Which tool would an architect likely leverage while diagnosing issues with an inbound RESTful integration to Salesforce?
optionA: Metadata audit trail
optionB: Force.com SOAP Explorer
optionC: Data Loader
optionD: Workbench
explanation:
Workbench lets you execute REST calls interactively, inspect requests and responses, and explore the API, which is what diagnosing an inbound RESTful integration needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (metadata audit trail) — records setup changes, not API traffic.
Option B (Force.com SOAP Explorer) — aimed at SOAP, so it cannot exercise a REST endpoint.
Option C (Data Loader) — moves records in bulk; it neither issues arbitrary REST calls nor shows you the responses.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/apex_integration_services/apex_integration_webservices

question: An Architect is asked to build a solution that allows a service to access Salesforce through the API. What is the first thing the Architect should do?
optionA: Authenticate the integration using existing Network-BasedSecurity.
optionB: Create a new user with System Administrator profile.
optionC: Create a special user solely for the integration purposes.
optionD: Authenticate the integration using existing Single Sign-On.
explanation:
Before granting a service API access, create a dedicated integration user with a least-privilege profile used solely for that integration, so its permissions are scoped and its activity is attributable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (authenticate with existing network-based security) — an IP control that says where a caller connects from, not who it is, and it grants nothing on its own.
Option B (new user with the System Administrator profile) — the opposite of least privilege: the service would hold every permission in the org.
Option D (authenticate using existing Single Sign-On) — SSO is designed for interactive human logins, not for a service, and it obscures which system acted.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.integration_user.htm&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2024/02/invoke-rest-apis-with-the-salesforce-integration-user-and-oauth-client-credentials

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) is looking to integrate three external systems that run nightly data enrichment processes in Salesforce. NTO has both of the following security and strict auditing requirements: 1. The external systems must follow the principle of least privilege, and 2. The activities of the eternal systems must be available for audit. What should an Integration Architect recommend as a solution for these integrations?
optionA: A shared integration user for the three external system integrations.
optionB: A shared Connected App for the three external system integrations.
optionC: A Connected App for each external system integration.
optionD: A unique integration user for each external system integration.
explanation:
Least privilege is enforced through the profile and permission sets of the identity a callout runs as, and the audit trail — LastModifiedBy, field history, login history — records that user. Giving each external system its own integration user satisfies both requirements at once.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (one shared integration user) — every system inherits the union of permissions the others need, and every record shows the same actor, defeating both requirements.
Option B (one shared Connected App) — a Connected App governs OAuth: which app may connect and with what scopes. Sharing one gives no separation at all.
Option C (a Connected App per system) — closer, but three apps authenticating as one shared user still grant each system that user's full permissions and still blur attribution.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.integration_user.htm&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2024/02/invoke-rest-apis-with-the-salesforce-integration-user-and-oauth-client-credentials

corrected.note: Q131 C->D. Least privilege and audit attribution come from distinct users, not from Connected Apps.

question: Universal Containers has a customer setup process that relies on external database to send customers welcome & registration emails. When a customer contacts Universal containers via phone, they need to receive the welcome email shortly following the conversation with the UC representative. Universal containers representatives work exclusively in Salesforce and any new customer contacts are created in Salesforce by the representative. The external database exposes a SOAP API for integration with other applications. What Salesforce technology best fulfills this requirement?
optionA: Write a trigger with an @future method to send customer Information to the external database
optionB: Write an outbound message to send customer Information to the external database.
optionC: Write an outbound message to send customer Information to an ESB.
optionD: Write a nightly batch synchronization to send customer information to the external database.
explanation:
The new customer must receive the welcome email shortly after the call, and the external system exposes a SOAP API, so a declarative workflow outbound message sends the customer information on contact creation without any code.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (trigger with an @future method) — custom development to achieve what outbound messaging does declaratively against a SOAP endpoint.
Option C (outbound message to an ESB) — adds a middleware hop that this single point-to-point requirement does not need.
Option D (nightly batch synchronisation) — far too slow for an email that must follow the phone call.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An enterprise architect has requested the Salesforce Integration architect to review the following (see diagram & description) and provide recommendations after carefully considering all constraints of the enterprise systems and Salesforce platform limits. * About 3,000 phone sales agents use a Salesforce Lightning UI concurrently to check eligibility of a customer for a qualifying offer. * There are multiple eligibility systems that provides this service and are hosted externally. However, their current response times could take up to 90 seconds to process and return (there are discussions to reduce the response times in future, but no commitments are made). * These eligibility systems can be accessed through APIs orchestrated via ESB (MuleSoft). * All requests from Salesforce will have to traverse through customer's API Gateway layer and the API Gateway imposes a constraint of timing out requests after 9 seconds. Which three recommendations should be made? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Implement a 'Check Update' button that passes a requestID received from ESB (user action needed).
optionB: Recommend synchronous Apex call-outs from Lightning UI to External Systems via Mule and implement polling on API gateway timeout.
optionC: ESB (Mule) with cache/state management to return a requestID (or) response if available from external system.
optionD: When responses are received by Mule, create a Platform Event in Salesforce via Remote-Call-In and use the empAPI in the lightning UI to serve 3,000 concurrent users.
optionE: Use Continuation callouts to make the eligibility check request from Salesforce from Lightning UI at page load.
explanation:
With eligibility responses of up to 90 seconds behind a gateway that times out at 9, no design can hold a single call open for the answer. The three keyed recommendations work as one architecture. C is the foundation: the ESB holds the state and answers every inbound request immediately — a requestID while the check is still running, or the cached response once it arrives. E is then safe: a Continuation at page load issues the request without holding an Apex thread, and because the ESB replies at once it returns well inside the 9-second window. A closes the loop, re-sending the requestID from a Check Update button.
Read E alone and it can look wrong, because a Continuation does not extend anyone else's timeout — its own ceiling is 120 seconds on the Salesforce side, and the timeout in the request object is ignored. What it buys is thread release, so many agents can have requests in flight without exhausting the concurrent long-running request limit. E is keyed because C guarantees the call it makes is a fast one.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (synchronous Apex callouts with polling on gateway timeout) — fails for the reason C exists: a plain synchronous callout waits on the eligibility system and dies at the 9-second gateway.
Option D (Platform Event via Remote-Call-In, consumed with empApi) — fails on a hard allocation, and the number is the thing to carry away. empApi uses one CometD connection per user session, and the cap on concurrent CometD clients across all channels is 2,000 on Performance and Unlimited, 1,000 on Enterprise, and 20 elsewhere. An option promising to serve 3,000 concurrent users this way exceeds the ceiling on every edition.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_continuation_overview.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_continuation_limits.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_event_limits.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lightning-component-reference/guide/lightning-emp-api.html

question: A healthcare services company maintains a Patient Prescriptions System that has 50+ million records in a secure database. Their customer base and data set growing rapidly. They want to make sure that the following policies are enforced: 1. Identifiable patient prescriptions must exist only in their secure system's database and encrypted at rest. 2. Identifiable patient prescriptions must be made available only to people explicit authorized in the Patient Prescriptions System assigned nurses and doctors, patient, and people explicitly the patient may authorize. 3. Must be available only to verified and pre-approved people or legal entities. To enable this, the company provides the following capabilities: 1. One-time use identity tokens for patients, nurses, doctors, and other people that expire within a few minutes. 2. Certificates for legal entities. . RESTful services. The company has a Salesforce Community Cloud portal for patients, nurses, doctors, and other authorized people. A limited number of employees analyze de identified data in Einstein Analytics. Which two capabilities should the integration architect require for the Community Cloud portal and Einstein Analytics? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Encryption in transit and at rest
optionB: Bulk load for Einstein Analytics
optionC: Callouts to RESTful services
optionD: Identity token data storage
explanation:
The question asks what these two components must be able to do. The Community portal cannot hold identifiable prescriptions, so it needs callouts to the secure system's RESTful services to fetch them on demand for an authorised user (C), and Einstein Analytics needs de-identified data bulk-loaded for the small analyst group (B).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (encryption in transit and at rest) — certainly required, but policy 1 already imposes it on the secure system; it is a baseline control rather than a capability the portal or Analytics has to provide.
Option D (identity token data storage) — would place identifiable material outside the secure database, breaking policy 1 outright.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.bi_dev_guide_ext_data.meta/bi_dev_guide_ext_data/bi_ext_data_overview.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_rest_exposing_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.named_credentials_about.htm&type=5

question: Universal learning (UC) is embarked on Salesforce transformation journey, UC will decommission the legacy CRM system and migrate data to Salesforce. The data migration team asked for a recommendation to optimize the performance of the dataload to Salesforce. Which approach should used to meet the requirement?
optionA: Contact Salesforce support to schedule performance load.
optionB: Use Bulk API to process jobs in parallel mode.
optionC: Use Bulk API to processjobs in high performance mode.
optionD: Use Bulk API to process jobs in serial mode.
explanation:
Bulk API in parallel mode processes multiple batches of a job concurrently, which is the highest-throughput route for a full legacy migration.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ask Salesforce Support to schedule a performance load) — reserved for genuinely extreme volumes, not a standard migration.
Option C (Bulk API in high performance mode) — no such mode exists; the choice is parallel or serial.
Option D (Bulk API in serial mode) — slower by design, and reserved for avoiding lock contention rather than for speed.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_asynch.meta/api_asynch/asynch_api_planning_guidelines.htm

question: Universal Containers has an integration that runs nightly to update the Product (Product2) object in Salesforce with updated product availability for over 500,000 products. The source system is green screen ERP that must be taken offline to produce nightly production reports such as the inventory availability report used for this integration. The Salesforce integration frequently reports failures due to data validation errors. Which two steps should the Technical Architect should recommend? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Ask the ERP report designers to redesign the report to provide properly formatted data.
optionB: Use SOAP headers to turn off validation rules and triggers during the integration.
optionC: Implements a regression testing policy to detect issues following development.
optionD: Review the Salesforce data model and Validation rules and modify the integration as necessary.
explanation:
Frequent validation failures on the nightly Product load point to a mismatch between the source data and Salesforce's rules, so review the data model and validation rules and adjust the integration to match (D), and put a regression-testing policy in place to catch what ongoing development breaks (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ask the ERP report designers to reformat the report) — may help at the margin, but it leaves the Salesforce-side rules unexamined, and the ERP is a green-screen system due to be worked around, not redesigned.
Option B (SOAP headers to disable validation rules and triggers) — no such header exists for arbitrary loads, and suppressing validation would let bad data in rather than fixing the mismatch.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_calls_update.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/data-cloud-dev/guide/dc-app-lifecycle.html

question: Universal Containers has a requirement to update the Salesforce Account object any time the corresponding account is updated within their financial system. Which three Salesforce capabilities should the Architect consider?
optionA: Enterprise WSDL because of a requirement to utilize SOAP-based services
optionB: Partner WSDL because of a requirement to utilize SOAP-based web services.
optionC: Partner WSDL because of a requirement to utilize REST-based web services
optionD: Partner WSDL because of a requirement to dynamically inspect field names during runtime.
optionE: Streaming API because of a requirement to dynamically inspect field names during runtime.
explanation:
The requirement is an inbound, SOAP-based update of the Salesforce Account whenever the financial system changes. The Enterprise WSDL gives a strongly typed, org-specific SOAP contract (A); the Partner WSDL gives a loosely typed one that works across orgs (B); and the Partner WSDL is also what allows field names to be inspected at runtime rather than compiled in, which matters when the payload varies (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Partner WSDL for REST-based web services) — misattributes the technology: a WSDL describes a SOAP service, not REST.
Option E (Streaming API for runtime field inspection) — pushes change notifications outward from Salesforce, which is both the wrong direction and unrelated to inspecting field names.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api.meta/api/sforce_api_partner.htm

question: An Architect has received a request to prevent employees that leave the company from accessing data in Salesforce after they are deactivated in the company's HR system. What should an Architect determine before recommending a solution?
optionA: Determine data volume requirements, then identify the loading schedule.
optionB: Determine inbound integration requirements, then identify frequency.
optionC: Determine data access prevention requirements, then identify system constraints.
optionD: Determine data access prevention requirements, then identify frequency.
explanation:
The architect has to pin down what "prevent access" means before designing anything — freezing, deactivating, stripping permission sets and handling in-flight sessions all imply different solutions — and then establish how quickly an HR deactivation must take effect. That frequency is what decides between event-driven propagation and a scheduled sync.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (data volume, then loading schedule) — the vocabulary of a migration; nothing here is about moving volumes of data.
Option B (inbound integration requirements, then frequency) — presumes an integration is the answer before the requirement it must satisfy is known.
Option C (access prevention requirements, then system constraints) — right first half, but constraints shape how you build it; the timing requirement is what selects the mechanism.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_deactivate_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Q139 B->D. Establish the access-prevention requirement first, then how fast it must propagate.

question: A company accepts payment requests 24x7. Once they accept a payment request, their service level agreement (SLA) requires them to make sure each payment request is processed by their Payment System. They track payment requests using a globally unique identifier created at the Data Entry Point. Their simplified flow is as shown in the diagram. They encounter intermittent update errors when two or more processes try to update the same Payment Request record at the same time. Which two recommendations should an integration architect make to improve their SLA and update conflict handling? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Payment System should process a payment request only once.
optionB: Data Entry Point and Middleware should automatically retry requests.
optionC: Payment System and Middleware should automatically retry requests.
optionD: Middleware should coordinate request delivery and payment processing.
explanation:
The globally unique identifier minted at the Data Entry Point is what lets the Payment System recognise a request it has already handled and process it exactly once, keeping the SLA without duplicate payments (A). The concurrent-update errors come from the fire-and-forget hop leaving no component in charge of ordering, so having the Middleware coordinate delivery and processing serialises the writes to a given record (D).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Data Entry Point and Middleware retry automatically) — resends requests that may still be in flight; without idempotency and coordination first, retries multiply both the duplicate processing and the contention.
Option C (Payment System and Middleware retry automatically) — the same objection, and retrying at the Payment System compounds the very duplication option A exists to prevent.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html

corrected.note: Q140 answer A,D confirmed against the diagram. The textual rendering added then was replaced on 2026-08-11 by a drawn sequence diagram, which puts both exchanges on one time axis.

question: Universal Containers (UC) sends Order data to an external ERP system via ESB. UC sends an outbound message on update or Order to ESB. Once ESB completes creating the Order in the back-end ERP, it send back the Order with the Order Number from the ERP. During development, UC is experiencing an issue. When the Order is updated by ESB, it again fires a workflow rule that sends the outbound message again. Which two recommended steps can be done to prevent this looping issue?
optionA: Write an Apex trigger to send an outbound message to ESB.
optionB: Update workflow rule conditions to exclude the ERP Order Number field update.
optionC: Update workflow rule conditions to exclude the Integration User.
optionD: Update the outbound message to exclude the Integration User.
explanation:
The loop exists because the ESB's write-back of the Order Number is itself an Order update, which re-satisfies the workflow rule and fires another outbound message. Both fixes narrow the rule so the write-back no longer qualifies: excluding the ERP Order Number field update makes the rule ignore the one field the ESB sets (B), and excluding the Integration User makes it ignore anything that identity does (C).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex trigger to send the outbound message) — rebuilds the same firing condition in code without removing the recursion, so the loop returns.
Option D (exclude the Integration User on the outbound message) — misplaces the filter: the outbound message defines what is sent, not when it fires.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.workflow_om_considerations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.workflow_managing_outbound_messages.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Q141 options B and E were identical and only one answer was marked on a two-answer question; deduped, answer B,C. (Found by validation, not by a comment.)

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a legacy homegrown application that stores customer data. Sales representatives edit contact records in Salesforce. UC has the following requirements: 1. Updates in Salesforce should update the homegrown application. 2. Synchronization should be event-driven. 3. The integration should be asynchronous. Which option should an architect recommend?
optionA: Leverage Change Data Capture to track changes to the Contact object and write a CometD subscriber on the homegrown application.
optionB: Leverage Platform Events to publish a custom event message containing changes to the Contact object.
explanation:
Change Data Capture is the mechanism to recommend. Its overview describes this scenario in one line — "receive near-real-time changes of Salesforce records, and synchronize corresponding records in an external data store" — and advises using it "instead of doing periodic exports and imports of data or repeated API calls". Enabling it on Contact publishes create, update, delete and undelete events to the ContactChangeEvent channel automatically, with no publishing code. The homegrown application subscribes as a CometD or Pub/Sub API client, satisfying all three requirements at once.
Note on this item: only two options were supplied with it. Read it as the two-way choice printed, rather than assuming a distractor was lost.
Why the other option is wrong:
Option B (Platform Events with a custom event message) — also event-driven and asynchronous, so this turns on which tool is purpose-built. A platform event is a message you design: you define it, publish it yourself from Apex, Flow or the API, and keep that logic in step with every field the external application needs. CDC carries the changed fields and change type for you. Choose Platform Events when the payload is a business event of your own design; choose CDC when, as here, it is simply "this record changed".
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.change_data_capture.meta/change_data_capture/cdc_subscribe_channels.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.platform_events.meta/platform_events/platform_events_intro.htm

question: Salesforce is the system of record for Leads, Contacts, Accounts, and Cases. Customer data also exists in an ERP system, a ticketing system, and a data lake, each of which identifies customers with its own unique identifier. Middleware is used to update the systems bidirectionally. Which solution should be recommended to handle this?
optionA: Design an MDM solution that maps external IDs to the Salesforce record ID.
optionB: Use Change Data Capture to update downstream systems accordingly.
optionC: Locally cache external IDs at the middleware layer.
explanation:
An MDM solution mapping each system's identifier onto the Salesforce record is right because the problem is identity, not delivery. Salesforce's integration-patterns guide frames data integration in those terms, naming master data management, mastering and de-duplication among the techniques that make it sustainable, and states the mechanic directly: "when integrating systems, unique record identifiers are important for ongoing state tracking". In practice that is an External Id field per source system, letting middleware upsert by foreign key instead of needing the Salesforce Id first.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Change Data Capture) — a delivery mechanism, not an identity strategy. It tells a subscriber a record changed; it does not say which ERP or ticketing row that record corresponds to, so the stated problem is untouched.
Option C (cache external IDs at the middleware layer) — the weakest of the three: it makes the middleware stateful, so the mapping drifts or is lost whenever it restarts, scales out or is replaced, and the cross-reference must then be rebuilt from systems that no longer agree.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#overview
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/dome_upsert.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters is creating a distributable Salesforce package. The package needs to call into a custom Apex REST endpoint in a central org. The security team wants to ensure a specific integration account is used in the central org, which they will authorize after the package is installed. Which item should an architect recommend?
optionA: Contact Salesforce Support and create a case to temporarily enable API access for managed packages.
optionB: Create a connected app in the central org and add the callback URL for each org the package is installed in, to redirect after a successful authentication.
optionC: Use an encrypted field to store the password that the security team enters.
explanation:
A connected app in the central org, with each subscriber org's callback URL registered, is the approach. The requirement — a named integration account in the central org, authorised after installation — is the OAuth 2.0 web server flow, and the redirect is what makes the post-install step work: the redirect URI must match a value in the Callback URL field, which accepts several URLs separated by line breaks up to 2,000 characters. Authorisation is then granted and revoked per subscriber org, the granularity the security team asked for.
Note on currency: connected app creation is restricted as of Spring '26 and Salesforce recommends external client apps for new work. Existing connected apps still function, and the mechanism here is unchanged.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (case with Salesforce Support to enable API access) — unnecessary: API access is a standard platform capability, not something Support enables per package.
Option C (encrypted field holding a password) — an anti-pattern that places a reusable credential in the subscriber org's data, gives no way to revoke one org without changing the credential for all, and forfeits OAuth's token expiry and scoping.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_create_api_integration.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_web_server_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) uses different shipping services for each of the 34 countries it serves. Services are added and removed frequently. Sales representatives globally need to select between the valid service(s) for the customer’s country and request shipping estimates. Which solution should an architect propose?
optionA: Store shipping services in a picklist that is dependent on a country picklist.
optionB: Invoke a middleware service to retrieve valid shipping methods.
optionC: Use Platform Events to construct and publish shipper-specific events.
explanation:
Calling a middleware service to return the valid shipping methods is right. Salesforce's integration-patterns guide assigns exactly these jobs to middleware — mediation routing, so "a mediator ensures that the right message reaches the right consumer", and transformation "to ensure interoperability" — and notes that "Salesforce doesn't support native protocol conversion", leaving it to the middleware layer, which often provides "service facades for legacy or other non-standard endpoints". With 34 carriers on their own protocols and a roster that changes frequently, that facade is the point: Salesforce makes one standard call carrying the country, and adding or dropping a carrier is a middleware change with no deployment in the org.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (dependent picklist of shipping services by country) — pushes the volatility into Salesforce metadata, so every carrier change is an admin edit, and it still leaves the callouts to 34 different APIs unsolved.
Option C (Platform Events publishing shipper-specific events) — the wrong pattern shape: the rep is waiting for an estimate during a live conversation, which is Request and Reply, whereas a platform event is asynchronous and returns nothing to the caller.
References:
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#overview
https://architect.salesforce.com/docs/architect/fundamentals/guide/integration-patterns.html#remote-process-invocation--request-and-reply

question: A business requires automating the check and updating of the phone number type classification (mobile vs. landline) for all incoming calls delivered to its phone sales agents. The following conditions exist: 1. At peak, the call center can receive up to 100,000 calls per day. 2. The phone number type classification is a service provided by an external service API. 3. The business is flexible with the timing and frequency of the check and update (overnight, or every 6-12 hours, is sufficient). A Remote-Call-In pattern and/or Batch Synchronization (replication via ETL from the external system into Salesforce) are determined to work, with middleware hosted on the customer’s premises. In order to implement these patterns and mechanisms, which component should an integration architect recommend?
optionA: A Connected App configured in Salesforce to authenticate the middleware.
optionB: An API Gateway that authenticates requests from Salesforce into the middleware (ETL/ESB).
optionC: Remote Site Settings configured in Salesforce to authenticate the middleware.
explanation:
A connected app is the component, because both named patterns have the middleware calling into Salesforce. Salesforce defines a connected app as "a framework that enables a third-party application to integrate with Salesforce by using APIs and standard protocols, such as SAML, OAuth, and OpenID Connect" — precisely this inbound case. It lets the on-premises ETL/ESB obtain a token, hold scoped permissions, and be audited and revoked as a distinct client; for an unattended job on a 6–12 hour cycle the JWT bearer flow is the usual pairing, authenticating as a designated integration user without storing a password.
Note on currency: connected app creation is restricted as of Spring '26 and Salesforce recommends external client apps for new builds. Existing connected apps still work, and the inbound-OAuth mechanism here is unchanged.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (API gateway authenticating requests from Salesforce into the middleware) — outbound-facing, and in these two patterns the traffic needing authentication runs the other way, into the org.
Option C (Remote Site Settings) — the opposite direction, and it authenticates nothing: it is only an allow-list of destinations Salesforce may call out to.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.connected_app_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.remoteaccess_oauth_jwt_flow.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_callouts_remote_site_settings.htm

question: A customer is evaluating the Platform Events solution and would like help comparing and contrasting it with Outbound Messaging for real-time / near-real-time needs. They expect 3,000 customers to view messages in Salesforce. What should be evaluated and highlighted when deciding between the solutions?
optionA: In both Platform Events and Outbound Messaging, the event messages are retried and delivered in sequence, and only once. Salesforce ensures there is no duplicate message delivery.
optionB: Message sequence is possible in Outbound Messaging, but not guaranteed with Platform Events. Both offer very high reliability. Fault handling and recovery are fully handled by Salesforce.
optionC: Both Platform Events and Outbound Messaging are highly scalable. However, unlike Outbound Messaging, only Platform Events have Event Delivery and Event Publishing limits to be considered.
explanation:
C is the consideration that matters, and its wording tracks the documentation: the Platform Events Developer Guide carries a section on default allocations for event publishing and delivery, governing how many events an org may publish and how many may be delivered to Pub/Sub, CometD, empApi and event relay subscribers. Outbound Messaging has no equivalent metering — it is a point-to-point SOAP push with a retry queue, not an event bus with allocations. For this customer the allocation to check first is the subscriber cap: concurrent CometD clients across all channels are limited to 2,000 on Performance and Unlimited and 1,000 on Enterprise. The stem's 3,000 viewers sit above every tier, so that number is the reason the comparison is worth making.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (both retry, deliver in sequence, and only once, with no duplicates) — contradicted outright. Of outbound messaging Salesforce says that "while each message is usually delivered one time, it can sometimes be delivered more than one time". Neither mechanism offers exactly-once delivery, so the receiving endpoint must be idempotent either way.
Option B (sequence guaranteed in Outbound Messaging but not Platform Events, recovery fully handled by Salesforce) — has the ordering backwards: outbound messages "are retried independent of their order in the queue... can be delivered out of order", while platform events carry a ReplayId marking position in the stream. Recovery is not fully handled by Salesforce either — the subscriber stores the replay ID and resubscribes within the 72-hour window.
