question: A Salesforce customer is planning to roll out Salesforce for all of their sales and service staff. Senior management has requested that monitoring be in place for Operations to be notified of any degradation in Salesforce performance. How should an integration consultant implement monitoring?
optionA: Use Salesforce API Limits to capture current API usage and configure alerts for monitoring.
optionB: Identify critical business processes and establish automation to monitor performance against established benchmarks.
optionC: Use ApiEvent to track all user-initiated API calls through SOAP, REST, or Bulk APIs.
explanation:
"Degradation in Salesforce performance" is a statement about what users experience, so the consultant starts from the critical business processes and a benchmark for each, then alerts on deviation. Salesforce's Well-Architected guidance frames performance the same way — throughput and latency, understood "through production testing and monitoring" — and makes it an architect responsibility to identify the business-critical use cases to scale-test, assessed "from the perspective of your customers". A process that normally takes two seconds and starts taking ten is a degradation; a number on a limits page is not.
On how firmly this is settled: the keyed answer is an operations practice rather than a platform fact, so the reference is orienting rather than decisive. What the documentation does settle is that the other two options measure something else.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (API limits usage with alerts) — measures quota consumption against the 24-hour allocation, which can run high while everything responds quickly, and low while a critical process crawls.
Option C (ApiEvent to track all user-initiated API calls) — narrower than the option admits: it tracks query(), queryMore() and count() only, and excludes Tooling API calls and calls from a Salesforce mobile app. It is built for security forensics, not for noticing a slowdown — and the word "all" is the part that makes the option false.

question: A US business-to-consumer (B2C) company is planning to expand to Latin America. They project an initial Latin American customer base of about one million, and a growth rate of around 10% every year for the next 5 years. They anticipate privacy and data protection requirements similar to those in the European Union to come into effect during this time. Their initial analysis indicates that key personal data is stored in the following systems: (1) legacy mainframe systems that have remained untouched for years and are due to be decommissioned; (2) Salesforce Commerce Cloud, Service Cloud, Marketing Cloud, and Community Cloud. The company's CIO has tasked the integration architect with ensuring that they can completely delete their Latin American customers' personal data on demand. Which three requirements should the integration architect consider? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Manual steps and procedures that may be necessary.
optionB: Impact of deleted records on system functionality.
optionC: Ability to delete personal data in every system.
optionD: Feasibility to restore deleted records when needed.
optionE: Ability to provide a 360-degree view of the customer.
explanation:
A, B and C are the requirements a delete-on-demand obligation actually generates. C is stated outright: "You must submit data deletion requests in every connected system and Salesforce cloud", and the stem names four Salesforce clouds plus the legacy mainframes, each with its own published deletion procedure. A follows from the mainframes: the platform deletion guidance is written almost entirely in manual steps, and a system untouched for years and already scheduled for decommissioning is unlikely to expose a deletion API at all. B is documented on that same page — refreshing a sandbox to clear data carries the warning that "work may be lost", and Event Monitoring logs "are treated as a single entity, which means you can't remove one single user's data from a log".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option D (feasibility to restore deleted records) — the trap, and the exact inverse of the requirement. Restorability is the platform default that complete deletion must defeat: deleted items sit in the Recycle Bin for 15 days and "can be restored", which is why Bulk API hard delete exists to bypass it. Compliance means removing the ability to restore, not preserving it.
Option E (360-degree view of the customer) — a benefit of integrating customer data, not a requirement of erasing it.
